hiragasy.name: Hiragasy
hiragasy.tagline: Merina highland spectacle of oratory, song and acrobatic dance
hiragasy.profile: Hiragasy (hira gasy, 'Malagasy song'; also vakodrazana) is a day-long musical spectacle and competition of the Merina of Madagascar's central highlands around Antananarivo, combining music, kabary oratory, singing and dance by costumed troupes (mpihira gasy) (Wikipedia; UNESCO). A performance follows a fixed structure - a sasitehaka prelude, kabary oration, songs, acrobatic dihy dance, and a closing vakodrazana; it generally involves two troupes and lasts about one hour and thirty minutes (UNESCO ICH, Hiragasy RL/01740). Costumes borrow red tunics, epaulettes and brass instruments from European military dress.
hiragasy.insight: Hiragasy was codified in the late 18th century by Merina sovereign Andrianampoinimerina, who hired musicians to rally dyke- and rice-field builders and to draw crowds for his kabary speeches; UNESCO inscribed it in 2023 at the 18th session (18.COM) in Kasane, Botswana (UNESCO ICH, RL/01740).

mapouka.name: Mapouka
mapouka.tagline: Tanzania, 1991 — Mapouka (or macouka,"la danse du fessier", or "the dance of the behind"), also known as Chura, or Baikoko i…
mapouka.profile: Mapouka (or macouka,"la danse du fessier", or "the dance of the behind"), also known as Chura, or Baikoko in Southern Africa, is a modernized version of a traditional dance from the Dabou area of southeast Côte d'Ivoire originating from the Ahizi, Alladian, Dida and Avikam people; it is also especially popular in Tanzania. Mapouka entered the music scene in 1991 following the 1990s creation of zouglou music and the importation of foreign music genres such as dancehall and hip hop, and grew in popularity, especially among the youth.
mapouka.insight: In March 1998, following complaints from citizens and women's rights groups, the government of Côte d'Ivoire banned Mapouka from public and television for being "sexually perverted, lewd and obscene".

hunguhungu.name: Hunguhungu
hunguhungu.era: Post-1797 Garifuna diaspora in Central America; rooted in St. Vincent culture (1635 ethnogenesis)
hunguhungu.tagline: Women's swaying circular dance in triple time, secular echo of the sacred dügü.
hunguhungu.profile: Hunguhungu (also 'hüngühüngü' or 'fedu') is a circular swaying dance performed chiefly by Garifuna women, distinctive for being in 3/4 (triple) meter rather than the usual duple-time Garifuna rhythms. Dancers form circles or lines, swaying their hips side to side while singing call-and-response, accompanied by the primero (treble) and segunda (bass) drums plus gourd shakers (sísira). It is described as the secular version of the adugurahani, the sacred drum/dance form of the dügü ancestor ceremony (English Wikipedia; Smithsonian Folkways).
hunguhungu.insight: Hunguhungu is a vehicle for women's communal expression and social commentary, with lyrics addressing loss, current events and community concerns; it falls under the UNESCO 2001/2008 inscription of Garifuna language, dance and music (English Wikipedia; UNESCO).

mwanzele.name: Mwanzele
mwanzele.tagline: Mijikenda/Giriama coastal funeral dance of Kenya
mwanzele.profile: Mwanzele is a dance style originally performed during funerals by the Mijikenda (notably the Giriama) people of Kenya's coastal region (Wikipedia). Described as a slow, poetic dance performed by elders, it is accompanied by songs telling stories of history, wisdom and life lessons. Popular performers include the late Bini Ya Mama and Bin Hare, while Mohamed Ngana ('Nyerere wa Konde') of the Malindi area became a leading composer who used the genre for public-health messaging.
mwanzele.insight: Mwanzele is a building block of coastal 'bango' music, a fusion of jazz, rhumba and Mijikenda traditional styles; its singers shifted from performing for fame to professional, recorded careers in recent decades (Wikipedia; Jumuiya News).

niiko.name: Niiko
niiko.tagline: n Ethnic minority of foreign descent in Somalia
niiko.profile: Niiko is a type of dance practiced by the Somali Bantus who are an Ethnic minority of foreign descent in Somalia. Due to its sensual nature it is more often done by non-practicing Muslims and eschewed by those who are religiously observant, and Somalis in general. Associate [Niiko] with the minority Bantu, who are descended from pre-Somali populations and recent immigrant eastern Swahili groups originally brought to Somalia as slaves... Niiko is therefore not necessarily an authentic Somali dance, but one that has been appropriated from minority cultures of African and slave descent.

punta.name: Punta
punta.era: Garifuna pre-1797 St. Vincent · Modern Honduran-Belizean
punta.tagline: The Garifuna people's signature dance — hips driving at impossible speed to garaon drum, the Afro-Indigenous Caribbean heartbeat.
punta.profile: Punta is the foundational dance of the Garifuna people — the Afro-Indigenous Caribbean nation descended from West African and Carib-Arawak peoples who fled to St. Vincent before being forcibly resettled to Honduras's Bay Islands in 1797 by the British. Today the Garifuna communities of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala, and Nicaragua keep punta alive at every wake, wedding, and celebration. The dance is centred on rapid hip articulations and weight transfers (men and women dancing solo or facing partners) to the polyrhythmic beat of the garaon (large skin drum), often combined with shaker and turtle-shell percussion.
punta.insight: In 2001, UNESCO proclaimed the Garifuna language and culture to be "a masterpiece of oral and intangible heritage of humanity", in recognition of the risk of an endangered status and loss of such an interesting culture.
sources: Source: Punta on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punta

ohangla.name: Ohangla
ohangla.era: Traditional; modern popular form since late 20th century
ohangla.tagline: Fast, drum-driven Luo dance and popular music
ohangla.profile: Ohangla is a traditional dance and musical style of the Luo community of western Kenya, built around a set of more than eight drums played with sticks plus a shoulder-slung cylindrical drum, often accompanied by a flute, nyatiti or orutu (Wikipedia). Historically performed at weddings and at funeral ceremonies (part of Tero Buru), it featured very fast tempos and frank lyrics; local elders banned it in the early 1980s as adult-only. It has since been revitalised into a hugely popular modern genre.
ohangla.insight: Modern Ohangla now cuts across age groups and ethnic lines - performers such as Tony Nyadundo and Prince Indah have made it a fixture at weddings, festivals and political rallies far beyond the Luo community (Wikipedia).

rebita.name: Rebita
rebita.tagline: Traditional Angolan couples ballroom dance, ancestor of semba.
rebita.profile: Rebita (also Massemba) is a traditional Angolan music and dance from Luanda in which a circle of couples, led by a 'commander' (Commandante) who calls directions, dance the umbigada-based Massemba movement, often to bands with concertina/accordion, horns and guitars. It contributed to the development of semba. Massemba was carried by enslaved Africans to Brazil, influencing umbigada, lundu and ultimately samba (English Wikipedia).
rebita.insight: Angola included Massemba/Rebita within a UNESCO ICH nomination process ('Semba: music and dance in Angola'); the umbigada belly-touch is the shared root linking Rebita to Brazilian samba (English Wikipedia; UNESCO).

zaouli.name: Zaouli
zaouli.tagline: Guro masked solo dance honouring feminine beauty
zaouli.profile: Zaouli is a masked solo dance of the Guro people of central Cote d'Ivoire (Bouafle and Zuenoula areas), created in the 1950s and named after a girl, 'Djela Lou Zaouli.' Per UNESCO, which inscribed it in 2017, it unites sculpture (the wooden mask), weaving (the costume), music and dance; a single male dancer, his upper body almost still beneath a striped costume, executes dazzlingly rapid, never-repeated footwork to flutes and drums. The mask is sacred, carved over days from yaranza wood, and only trained initiates may wear it.
zaouli.insight: Zaouli is celebrated as one of the world's most technically demanding dances and a unifying emblem of Guro and Ivorian identity; it gained national fame as a favourite of President Felix Houphouet-Boigny (UNESCO; Wikipedia).

seki-dance.name: Seki Dance
seki-dance.tagline: Nigeria — Seki Dance, also known as the Seki Dance Drama, is a type of performance dance that traces the roots of the…
seki-dance.profile: Seki Dance, also known as the Seki Dance Drama, is a type of performance dance that traces the roots of the American tap dance to the Indigenous people of the Niger Delta. This theatrical dance performance was created by Yibo Koko in Rivers State, Nigeria. Séki dance showcases the dances of the people of Niger Delta, Nigeria and how they came to be.
seki-dance.insight: The Seki was initially prepared as an entry for the 1998 Atlanta Georgia National Black Arts Festival, but got its premiere at the Eko Hotels and Suites, Lagos, on Saturday 26 March 2016, as commissioned by Heritage Bank Nigeria Plc.
sources: Source: Seki Dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seki_Dance

takamba.name: Takamba
takamba.tagline: Mali — music and dance native to the Songhai and Tuareg peoples of Niger and Mali
takamba.profile: Takamba is a music and dance native to the Songhai and Tuareg peoples of Niger and Mali. It is both a musical composition and a dance. The musicians play a traditional instrument known as the Kurbu or Tehardent and a traditional African Calabash. The Takamba dance includes graceful and rhythmic movements performed both seated and standing where the shoulders and arms sway with the flow of the music.
takamba.insight: Takamba is a music and dance native to the Songhai and Tuareg peoples of Niger and Mali.
sources: Source: Takamba on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takamba

latin-dance.name: Latin dance
latin-dance.era: Term formalized 20th century; roots Indigenous/European/African colonial era
latin-dance.tagline: Umbrella term for many Latin American social and ballroom dances.
latin-dance.profile: 'Latin dance' is a broad umbrella category, not a single dance. It has two meanings: (1) social/street Latin dances (salsa, mambo, merengue, rumba, bachata, bomba, plena) and (2) the competitive ballroom 'International Latin' category (cha-cha-cha, samba, rumba, paso doble, jive). It draws on Indigenous American, European, and African influences (English Wikipedia). Argentine folk dances (chacarera, gato, zamba) are generally NOT classed as 'Latin dance.'
latin-dance.insight: As a category, 'Latin dance' reflects the fusion of Native, European, and African traditions across Latin America and the codification of competitive ballroom Dancesport (English Wikipedia).

taskiwin.name: Taskiwin
taskiwin.tagline: Berber women's mountain dance of Morocco's Western High Atlas — UNESCO-protected as endangered heritage.
taskiwin.profile: Taskiwin (Berber languages: ⵜⴰⵙⴽⵉⵡⵉⵏ, Arabic: تاسكيوين) is a traditional dance of Morocco that is recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. It is a martial dance that is specific to the western High Atlas mountain range in central Morocco. The dance gets its name from the richly decorated horn each dancer carries, known as the Tiskt. The dance involves the art of shaking one's shoulders to the rhythm of tambourines and flutes, and stomping the feet.
taskiwin.insight: Taskiwin is a traditional dance of Morocco that is recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Since 1993, several local associations were created in an attempt to preserve this tradition.
sources: Source: Taskiwin on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taskiwin

tufo.name: Tufo
tufo.profile: Tufo is a traditional dance in Northern Mozambique. The dance is performed by groups of women and is found in Maputo, the provinces of Cabo Delgado and Nampula and the Island of Mozambique. Of Arab origin, the dance is performed to celebrate Islamic festivals and holidays. The dance is traditionally performed by dancers moving just the top halves of their bodies and accompanied by songs and tambourine-like drums.
tufo.insight:
== Performance ==
Historically tufo was performed by both male and female dancers but now men usually only dance on rare occasions.

cachucha.name: Cachucha
cachucha.tagline: Spain — Spanish solo dance in 34 or 38 time, similar to the bolero
cachucha.profile: Cachucha is a Spanish solo dance in 34 or 38 time, similar to the bolero. Cachucha is danced to an Andalusian national song with castanet accompaniment.
cachucha.insight: Fanny Elssler (1810-1884, Vienna) popularized this dance when she introduced it to the public in the ballet from Rossini's opera La donna del lago in 1830s London, and cemented its fame in Jean Coralli's ballet Le Diable boiteux (1836, Vienna).
sources: Source: Cachucha on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cachucha

guapacha.name: Guapacha
guapacha.tagline: Cuban rhythm/style related to the cha-cha-cha.
guapacha.profile: Guapacha (also 'wa-pa-cha') is a Cuban rhythm and social-dance style, a trendy variant of the guaracha/cha-cha-cha that peaked in the early 1960s. The Cuba Music Week genre database describes it as a trendy Cuban social dance based on the guaracha; on a Tito Rodriguez LP it was promoted as 'nothing more than the Cha Cha with clapping accompaniment.' In ballroom technique, 'guapacha timing' denotes a characteristic syncopation (delaying a step) applied within cha-cha-cha figures (Cuba Music Week; Wikibooks).
guapacha.insight: Guapacha survives less as an independent genre than as 'guapacha timing,' a syncopated rhythmic device used by cha-cha-cha dancers; it is also associated with the singer Amado Borcela, nicknamed 'Guapacha' (Wikibooks).

charikawi.name: Charikawi
charikawi.tagline: traditional mimed dance of the Garifuna, in which a hunter encounters a cave man and a cow
charikawi.profile: The charikawi is a traditional mimed dance of the Garifuna, in which a hunter encounters a cave man and a cow. The word may also refer to the music for such a dance.
charikawi.insight: The charikawi is a traditional mimed dance of the Garifuna, in which a hunter encounters a cave man and a cow.
sources: Source: Charikawi on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charikawi

beguine.name: Beguine
beguine.tagline: Italy — dance and music form, similar to a slow rhumba
beguine.profile: The beguine ( bə-GHEEN) is a dance and music form, similar to a slow rhumba. It was popular in the 1930s, coming from the islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique, where, in the local Antillean Creole language, beke or begue means a White man while beguine is the female form. It is a combination of Latin folk dance and French ballroom dance, and is a spirited yet slow, close dance with a roll of the hips, a movement inherited from rhumba. After Cole Porter wrote the song "Begin the Beguine", the dance became more widely known beyond the Caribbean.
beguine.insight: In 1984, Italian pop music duo Al Bano and Romina Power released the song "Al ritmo di beguine (Ti amo)" from their album Effetto amore.
sources: Source: Beguine (dance) on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beguine_(dance)

lambado-cuiabano.name: Lambadao cuiabano
lambado-cuiabano.tagline: Fast peripheral couples lambadao of Cuiaba, Mato Grosso.
lambado-cuiabano.profile: Lambadao cuiabano (or simply lambadao) is a music-and-dance style characteristic of the Baixada Cuiabana in Mato Grosso, especially Cuiaba and Varzea Grande. A fast, swinging rhythm of the urban periphery with romantic or playful lyrics, it arrived via Para prospectors who brought lambada and synthesizes Para lambada with the local rasqueado heritage. Its first boom came in the 1990s (English Wikipedia; Prefeitura de Cuiaba).
lambado-cuiabano.insight: Often marginalized outside the periphery for its more sexualized versions, lambadao is nonetheless protected by municipal (Cuiaba) and Mato Grosso state cultural laws (Prefeitura de Cuiaba).

danza.name: Danza (Cuba)
danza.profile: The Cuban danza was an early-19th-century creole ballroom dance and music form - a derivative of the contradanza (contradanza criolla / danza criolla / habanera). The oldest known Cuban danza, 'El Sungambelo,' dates to 1813. Unlike the figure-based contradanza, the danza introduced the closed couple-hold (influenced by the waltz), with slower, more relaxed movements and the characteristic habanera rhythm. It is a direct ancestor of the danzon (1879, Miguel Failde) and thus of mambo and cha-cha-cha (English Wikipedia: Contradanza; Peter Manuel, CUNY).
danza.insight: Per musicologist Argeliers Leon, the danza was musically near-identical to the contradanza but danced differently, marking the Cuban transition from communal sequence dances to independent couple dances (English Wikipedia: Contradanza).

bachatango.name: Bachatango
bachatango.tagline: Fusion of Dominican bachata with Argentine tango moves.
bachatango.profile: Bachatango is a fusion style combining the four-step Dominican bachata with Argentine tango elements - kicks, dips, turns, ganchos, leg wraps, and long pauses - characterized by sensual hip movements; partners hold a closed position with inner-thigh contact (English Wikipedia). It originated among dance instructors in Turin, Italy, was once popular in foreign ballrooms, and is now rare on social floors.
bachatango.insight: Bachatango exemplifies the early-2000s 'Bachata Fusion' trend in which dancers blended bachata with tango, salsa, and zouk; it is essentially unknown in the Dominican Republic, bachata's homeland (English Wikipedia).

brazilian-zouk.name: Brazilian Zouk
brazilian-zouk.tagline: Sensual partner dance evolved from lambada, danced to zouk.
brazilian-zouk.profile: Brazilian Zouk is a partner dance that began in Brazil in the early 1990s when lambada dancers, losing access to lambada music, adapted their movements to slower Caribbean zouk music (e.g. Kassav'). Structured for teaching at Jaime Aroxa's Rio school by Renata Pecanha and Adilio Porto, it features undulating upper-body movement, body isolations, tilted turns, dips and whip-like head movements. Main substyles: Traditional/Rio-style, Lambazouk (Porto Seguro), and Neo/Modern zouk (English Wikipedia).
brazilian-zouk.insight: The name distinguishes the Brazilian dance from Caribbean zouk music; today 'zouk' in dance contexts usually means Brazilian Zouk, danced worldwide (English Wikipedia).

latin-jam-workout.name: Latin Jam Workout
latin-jam-workout.tagline: Latin Dance Fitness Program created by professional athlete and choreographer JP Santana
latin-jam-workout.profile: Latin Jam Workout is a Latin Dance Fitness Program created by professional athlete and choreographer JP Santana. Founded in 2007 in Los Angeles, California, Latin Jam Workout combines techno and Latin music with dance and aerobic movements. It is a fusion of Latin dance steps such as Salsa, Merengue, Raeggaeton, Cumbia, Samba, Soca, Belly-Dancing and the faster-paced rhythms of Pop and Techno. Latin Jam Workout is taught in fitness venues, gyms, dance studios, schools and community centers by certified instructors.
latin-jam-workout.insight:
== History ==
Latin Jam Workout was created by JP Santana in Los Angeles, in 2009.
sources: Source: Latin Jam Workout on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Jam_Workout

guaracha.name: Guaracha
guaracha.profile: The guaracha is a Cuban genre of rapid tempo with comic, picaresque or satirical lyrics, documented since the late 18th/early 19th century. Played in musical theatres and working-class dance salons, it became integral to bufo comic theatre by the mid-19th century and was a favourite in Havana's brothels around 1900. Accompanied by guitar and tres (later by conjuntos and big bands), it uses soloist-coro call-and-response, combinations of 6/8 with 2/4, and slang-filled topical lyrics. It survives in trova, conjunto and salsa repertoires (English Wikipedia; Smithsonian).
guaracha.insight: During the 19th-century independence struggle, the bufo theatre's guarachas served as a political weapon, lampooning Spanish authorities and supporting Cuban independence (English Wikipedia).

juego-de-man.name: Juego de mani
juego-de-man.era: Clearly by the 19th c. on Cuban sugar plantations; Kongo-Angola roots
juego-de-man.tagline: Afro-Cuban combat dance, a Cuban cousin of capoeira.
juego-de-man.profile: Juego de mani (also mani, baile de mani, or bambosa) is a combined martial art and dance developed by enslaved Africans in Cuba, with roots in Kongo-Angola (Central African) culture. Historically popular in Matanzas and Las Villas, it featured circling, competitive male dancing in a ring; practitioners are maniseros. The rhythm is set by drummers, using the music of Palo Monte. Techniques include low kicks, foot sweeps, punches, elbow and palm strikes; sticks and machetes were sometimes used. It influenced non-combative social dances such as rumba columbia (English Wikipedia; Capoeira History, citing Fernando Ortiz 1951).
juego-de-man.insight: Scholars including Matthias Rohrig Assuncao note mani shares form and meaning with capoeira, supporting the view that African-derived combat games in the Americas shared common Kongo-Angola features (English Wikipedia).

sambai.name: Sambai
sambai.era: Rooted in 18th-c. Afro-Belizean Maroon/Creole culture (Gales Point Manatee); UNESCO-inscribed Dec 2025
sambai.tagline: Afro-Creole full-moon fertility and courtship dance around a bonfire.
sambai.profile: The sambai (also 'sambay') is a Creole/Kriol fertility dance from the village of Gales Point Manatee, performed during the full moon and at weddings or birthdays. Per Wikipedia (citing O'Donnell, Adventure Guide to Belize, 2002), it is a solitary dance originally performed by men but now by either gender: the dancer enters a ring of drummers to dance, and when finished points to another person who dances next. The National Kriol Council describes a circle gathered around a pinewood fire; music is led by the goombay (gumbeh) drum with call-and-response chants.
sambai.insight: The National Kriol Council notes the sambai's link to the full-moon cycle parallels lunar crop cycles, reinforcing its identity as a fertility ritual. It was inscribed by UNESCO in December 2025 (20.COM) as part of 'Christmas Bram and Sambai' (ICH no. 02298) - Belize's second inscription after the 2008 Garifuna listing (UNESCO; National Kriol Council).

sandungueo.name: Sandungueo
sandungueo.tagline: Puerto Rico — Sandungueo, also known as perreo, is a style of dance and party music associated with reggaeton that emerge…
sandungueo.profile: Sandungueo, also known as perreo, is a style of dance and party music associated with reggaeton that emerged in the late 1980s in Puerto Rico. The style was developed by DJ Blass, who released the albums Sandunguero Vol. 1 and Vol. 2, and it was further popularized worldwide through the website Sandungueo.com. Sandungueo is characterized by hip movements and can be performed in various ways. It may be danced solo or with a partner, with men and women often adopting different approaches.
sandungueo.insight: The Cuban government appeared to share this sentiment, banning reggaeton (sometimes referred to as "Cubaton") in 2012.
sources: Source: Sandungueo on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandungueo

peruvian-cumbia.name: Peruvian cumbia
peruvian-cumbia.profile: A Peruvian subgenre of cumbia that became popular in coastal cities, mainly Lima, in the 1960s, fusing Colombian cumbia with Andean huayno, Cuban percussion and psychedelic/surf rock; built on electric guitars, bass, organ/synthesizer and pentatonic Andean harmonies (Wikipedia). 'Chicha' is named after a corn-based liquor; pioneers include Los Destellos, Los Mirlos and Juaneco y Su Combo.
peruvian-cumbia.insight: This entry was mislabeled as Colombian in the source catalog; Peruvian cumbia is a distinct Peruvian genre derived from - but not the same as - Colombian cumbia (Wikidata Q7171184).

chhayam.name: Chhayam
chhayam.tagline: Khmer comic drum procession of clowns and clappers
chhayam.profile: Chhayam (ឆៃយ៉ាំ) is a traditional Khmer musical dance: a light-hearted, comedic processional form combining percussive rhythms, exaggerated movements, call-and-response singing and improvisation (Wikipedia; Dance in Cambodia). Male drummers play brightly decorated long drums (skor chhayam) with wooden clappers (krab) and cymbals, while comically painted male dancers flirt with a central graceful female dancer who ignores them; bystanders clap and sing along. It is performed at holidays, especially Khmer New Year, often to lead ceremonial processions.
chhayam.insight: Chhayam is regarded as a "pure Khmer" entertainment dance believed to bring good luck and happiness; it leads festival processions at Chaul Chnam Thmey and has been sustained in diaspora communities (e.g., Long Beach and Lowell, USA) to pass Khmer heritage to younger generations (Dance in Cambodia, Wikipedia).

biyelgee.name: Biyelgee
biyelgee.tagline: Mongolia's body dance — UNESCO-listed Urgent Safeguarding tradition where the dancer's body becomes the steppe itself.
biyelgee.profile: Biyelgee (Mongolian Cyrillic: Биелгээ) or Bii (Mongolian Cyrillic: Бий), is a traditional dance from Mongolia. Most of the country's regions have their own forms. The Western Mongols (Oirats) are particularly famous for their Biyelgee dance.
biyelgee.insight: UNESCO inscribed Biyelgee on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding in 2009 — recognising that the tradition was at risk as Mongolia urbanised away from its nomadic roots. The dance's defining feature is its constraint: performed inside a ger with no floor space, every movement is from the waist up, with the body retelling a pastoral life — milking the goats, drawing the bow, riding the horse — through pure upper-body gesture.

anyeint.name: Anyeint
anyeint.tagline: Thailand — Anyeint (Burmese: အငြိမ့်, MLCTS: a ngrim
anyeint.profile: Anyeint (Burmese: အငြိမ့်, MLCTS: a ngrim.; IPA: [ʔəɲḛiɰ̃]; Burmese: အငြိမ့်; also spelt a-nyeint) is a traditional Burmese entertainment form that combines dance with instrumental music, song, and comedy routines, in theatrical performances. It is a form of pwe, the Burmese word for traditional entertainment. While classical pwe can be quite formal and almost ritualistic, anyeint is considered light entertainment.
anyeint.insight: The first known anyeint troupe was formed in Mandalay around 1900, by comedian U Chit Phwe and his wife, dancer Ma Sein Thone.
sources: Source: Anyeint on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyeint

burmese-dance.name: Burmese dance
burmese-dance.tagline: Thailand, 1989 — Dance in Burma (since 1989 known as Myanmar) can be divided into dramatic, folk and village, and nat dances…
burmese-dance.profile: Dance in Burma (since 1989 known as Myanmar) can be divided into dramatic, folk and village, and nat dances, each having distinct characteristics. Although Burmese dance resemble the traditional dancing style of its neighbors, in particular Thailand, it retains unique qualities that distinguish it from other regional styles, including angular, fast-paced and energetic movements and emphasis on pose, not movement.
burmese-dance.insight: However, in their first act, the two brothers used their new powers to pay back the Count in his own coin, causing the Count's murder and his return as the Nat U Min Gyaw.
sources: Source: Burmese dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burmese_dance

samba-de-gafieira.name: Samba de Gafieira
samba-de-gafieira.tagline: Rio's elegant ballroom partner samba, the 'Brazilian tango'.
samba-de-gafieira.profile: Samba de Gafieira is a Brazilian ballroom partner dance (danca de salao) that emerged in 1940s Rio de Janeiro in working-class dance halls called gafieiras. Evolving from maxixe and later absorbing Argentine tango influence, it features the passo basico, saida lateral, leg adornments and (in performance) acrobatic figures. A unified teaching syllabus was agreed by Rio teachers in 2001 (English Wikipedia; Atomic Ballroom).
samba-de-gafieira.insight: Distinct from international ballroom Samba, it is sometimes called the 'Brazilian tango'; danced to samba, choro, pagode and other rhythms (English Wikipedia).

gombhira.name: Gombhira
gombhira.era: Traditional (post-7th/8th c.; modern form ~150 years old)
gombhira.tagline: Malda's satirical Shiva folk-theatre of dance and song
gombhira.profile: Gombhira (also Gambhira/Gamvira) is a traditional Bengali folk performing art of the Malda district of West Bengal, combining musical theatre, dance, song and satire to address social and regional issues, typically performed by all-male troupes during Shiva-worshipping festivals (Wikipedia; MAP Academy). Its name derives from 'gombhir' (poise/gravity), a quality associated with Shiva; performances traditionally took place between April and June as part of Chaitra Sankranti / Gajan celebrations (MAP Academy). A typical performance unfolds in stages - bandana (invocation to Shiva), dwaita (duet), charyaari, palabandi gaan (provocation) and khabar (reporting) - and in its classic form two performers, one representing Shiva, converse about everyday hardships (Indian Culture portal).
gombhira.insight: Gombhira evolved from the song-and-dance forms of the Koch people of the Malda region and is tied to local mango cultivation and Shiva worship; it survives in Malda and Murshidabad in India and in Dinajpur, Rangpur and Rajshahi in Bangladesh, where grandfather-and-grandson figures critique sociopolitical issues (MAP Academy; Wikipedia).

bhairab-naach.name: Bhairab Naach
bhairab-naach.tagline: Nepal — Bhaila Pyankhan, or "Bhairava's Dance" is an traditional masked dance performed by Newar community in the P…
bhairab-naach.profile: Bhaila Pyankhan, or "Bhairava's Dance" is an traditional masked dance performed by Newar community in the Pokhara Valley of Nepal as part of the Bhairab Jatra festival and named after Bhairab, an aspect of Shiva.

peacock-dance.name: Peacock dance
peacock-dance.tagline: Ambiguous - Indian Mayil Attam vs Dai/Chinese peacock dance
peacock-dance.profile: 'Peacock dance' is ambiguous. In India it most plausibly refers to Mayil Attam (Peacock Dance) of Tamil Nadu, a temple folk dance in which performers dress in peacock costumes with beaks and dance in honour of Lord Murugan (whose vehicle is the peacock). However, the better-known 'Peacock dance' internationally is the Dai/Chinese peacock dance (kongque wu), which is filed elsewhere under China; the present India filing therefore risks duplicating that entry. No single reliable Wikipedia article/QID is assigned without clarifying which dance is intended.
peacock-dance.insight: If this slug is meant as an Indian dance, it should map to Mayil Attam (Tamil Nadu); if it carries over the Dai/Chinese peacock dance, it duplicates a China entry - this must be disambiguated before finalising.

kushtdepdi.name: Kushtdepdi
kushtdepdi.tagline: Turkey, 2017 — form of performing arts characteristic of Turkmenistani culture, combining improvised poetry, dance, and song
kushtdepdi.profile: Küştdepdi is a form of performing arts characteristic of Turkmenistani culture, combining improvised poetry, dance, and song. Küştdepdi has been preserved as a ritual and entertainment component of traditional celebrations. In 2017, the tradition was inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in English as the Kushtdepdi rite of singing and dancing and in Turkmen as Küştdepdi aýdym we tans dessury.
kushtdepdi.insight:
== International recognition ==
On December 7, 2017, the Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in Jeju, South Korea, unanimously inscribed the Kushtdepdi rite of singing and dancing on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Lists.

sogdian-whirl-dance.name: Sogdian Whirl dance
sogdian-whirl-dance.era: first half 1st millennium CE; peak Tang dynasty
sogdian-whirl-dance.tagline: Spinning Silk Road dance of whirling Sogdian performers
sogdian-whirl-dance.profile: The Sogdian Whirl (胡旋, Húxuán) was a Central Asian dance imported into China in the first half of the first millennium CE, in which a dancer spun rapidly within a small circle on a round carpet (English Wikipedia). Especially popular in Tang Chang'an and Luoyang, it was performed at court — reputedly by Yang Guifei and An Lushan — and is depicted in Sogdian and Chinese funerary art and Dunhuang murals (Smithsonian; CGTN).
sogdian-whirl-dance.insight: Celebrated in Bai Juyi's poem 'The Whirling Girl,' the dance symbolizes the cosmopolitan, outward-looking spirit of the Tang dynasty and Silk Road cultural exchange (Smithsonian 'The Sogdians'; China Daily).

sanni-yakuma.name: Sanni Yakuma
sanni-yakuma.tagline: Sanni yakuma, sometimes known as Daha ata sanniyas, is a traditional Sinhalese exorcism ritual
sanni-yakuma.profile: Sanni yakuma, sometimes known as Daha ata sanniyas, is a traditional Sinhalese exorcism ritual. The ritual consists of 18 masked dances, each depicting a particular illness or ailment affecting humans. These 18 dances are the main dances of the Pahatharata, country, dancing form, which is one of the three main dancing forms of Sri Lanka. The ritual calls the demons who are thought to affect the patient, who are then told not to trouble humans and banished.
sanni-yakuma.insight:
=== Ata Paliya ===
Ata Paliya is the name given to the eight dances in the first stage of the ritual.
sources: Source: Sanni Yakuma on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanni_Yakuma

balos.name: Balos
balos.tagline: Greece — traditional folk dance of Greece, from the island of Kythnos
balos.profile: Balos or Ballos of Kythnos (Greek: : Μπάλος της Κύθνου or Θερμιώτικος μπάλος) is a traditional folk dance of Greece, from the island of Kythnos. It is performed by both men and women.
balos.insight: Balos or Ballos of Kythnos (Greek: : Μπάλος της Κύθνου or Θερμιώτικος μπάλος) is a traditional folk dance of Greece, from the island of Kythnos.

bacchu-ber.name: Bacchu-ber
bacchu-ber.profile: The bacchu-ber (French: [ba.ky.bɛʁ]), derived from Occitan bau cubèrt (Occitan: [baw ky'bɛʁ], covered dance or indoor ball), is a traditional folk dance performed with swords. This dance takes place in the district of Pont-de-Cervières, city of Briançon (Hautes-Alpes, France). Its origin dates back to many centuries ago (first written confirmation in 1730). This folk dance is unique in France and is one of the rare sword dances that have stood the test of time. It is performed once a year on 16 August, day of Saint Roch (1340–1379), patron of the Pont-de-Cervières district.
bacchu-ber.insight: In 2003, for a commemoration, the Bacchu-ber was exceptionally performed by 2 circles of dancers (usually only one).

sword-dance.name: Sword dance
sword-dance.tagline: Yorkshire — dancers weave swords into a six-pointed lock star, raised over the lead dancer's neck. A failed lock means symbolic beheading.
sword-dance.profile: Weapon dances incorporating swords or similar weapons are recorded throughout world history. There are various traditions of solo and mock-battle sword dances in Africa, Asia and Europe. Some traditions use sticks or clubs in place of bladed weapons, while most modern performers employ dulled replications to avoid injury.
sword-dance.insight: mock-battle dances, including many stick dances from non-sword traditions, and such common continental dances as Bouffons or Mattachins as described by Thoinot Arbeau in 1588.

huteng.name: Huteng
huteng.tagline: Acrobatic Sogdian 'leaping' dance of the Silk Road
huteng.profile: Huteng (胡腾, Húténg, 'Nomadic/barbarian leap') was a Central Asian dance, especially of the Sogdians and the region of Tashkent (Shiguo), well known in Tang-dynasty China (English Wikipedia). It was characterized by spinning, leaps and backflips: dancers planted their feet on a small carpet, arched their bodies and jumped backward to flutes and the pipa. It is depicted in Tang tomb murals and figurines.
huteng.insight: Together with the Sogdian Whirl, Huteng exemplifies the cosmopolitan exchange along the Silk Road that enriched Tang court and folk performing arts (Smithsonian 'The Sogdians'; English Wikipedia).

barn-dance.name: Barn dance
barn-dance.tagline: Ireland — ny kind of dance involving traditional or folk music with traditional dancing, occasionally held in a barn,…
barn-dance.profile: A barn dance is any kind of dance involving traditional or folk music with traditional dancing, occasionally held in a barn, but, these days, much more likely to be in any suitable building. The term "barn dance" is usually associated with family-oriented or community-oriented events, usually for people who do not normally dance. The caller will, therefore, generally use easy dances so that everyone can join in. A barn dance can be a ceilidh, with traditional Irish or Scottish dancing, and people unfamiliar with either format often confuse the two terms.
barn-dance.insight: The National Barn Dance began as a program of old-time fiddling on April 19, 1924, with George D.

bulgarian-folk-dance.name: Bulgarian folk dance
bulgarian-folk-dance.era: Pre-Christian/Thracian roots; systematically collected from the 19th century
bulgarian-folk-dance.tagline: The umbrella tradition of Bulgarian chain/line dancing.
bulgarian-folk-dance.profile: The broad category of Bulgarian folk dance, overwhelmingly built on the horo (хоро) chain/line dance plus the solo/couple rachenitsa. Defined by asymmetrical 'Bulgarian rhythms' (short=2, long=3 units) producing 5/8, 7/8, 9/8, 11/16, 13/16 and 15/16 meters across seven ethnographic regions. Handholds include the V (down), W (shoulder height), shoulder hold and belt-hold (na lesa). Instruments: gaida, gadulka, kaval, tambura and tapan. Danced at weddings, holidays and village gatherings (English Wikipedia; Britannica).
bulgarian-folk-dance.insight: Ethnomusicologist Timothy Rice's fieldwork found each generic dance name is tied to a unique repeating pattern of unequal short and long beats; the national repertoire is commonly cited at ~300 chain dances (Radio Bulgaria/BNR, quoting the Taratanci Foundation).

chapelloise.name: Chapelloise
chapelloise.profile: The Chapelloise (French pronunciation: [\ʃa.pɛ.lwaz\] ) is a traditional folk dance with change of partners (a so-called mixer), belonging to the standard repertoire of a Balfolk. Its most common name in France and the French-influenced European Balfolk scene is Chapelloise, but the dance has many other names in different countries.
chapelloise.insight: It is often claimed that the dance is of Swedish origin and that its original name is “Aleman's marsj” (Guilcher 1998, Oosterveen 2002, Largeaud 2011 and countless websites).
sources: Source: Chapelloise on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapelloise

circle-dance.name: Circle dance
circle-dance.tagline: Circle dance, or chain dance, is a style of social dance done in a circle, semicircle or a curved line to m…
circle-dance.profile: Circle dance, or chain dance, is a style of social dance done in a circle, semicircle or a curved line to musical accompaniment, such as rhythm instruments and singing, and is a type of dance where anyone can join in without the need of partners. Unlike line dancing, circle dancers are in physical contact with each other; the connection is made by hand-to-hand, finger-to-finger or hands-on-shoulders, where they follow the leader around the dance floor. Ranging from gentle to energetic, the dance can be an uplifting group experience or part of a meditation.
circle-dance.insight: Derived from a medieval ring dance, and surviving only in the Faroes, it is danced traditionally in a circle, but when a lot of people take part in the dance they usually let it swing around in various wobbles within the circle.
sources: Source: Circle dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_dance

country-dance.name: Country dance
country-dance.tagline: France — repeated execution of a predefined sequence of figures, carefully designed to fit a fixed length of music, …
country-dance.profile: A country dance is any of a very large number of social dances of a type that originated in England in the British Isles; it is the repeated execution of a predefined sequence of figures, carefully designed to fit a fixed length of music, performed by a group of people, usually in couples, in one or more sets. The figures involve interaction between partners and with other dancers, usually with a progression so that each participant dances with everyone in the set. It is common in modern times to have a "caller" who teaches the dance and then calls the figures during the dance.
country-dance.insight: In 1706 Raoul Auger Feuillet published his Recüeil de Contredances, a collection of "contredanses anglaises" presented in a simplified form of Beauchamp-Feuillet notation and including some dances invented by the author as well as authentic English dances.
sources: Source: Country dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_dance

cornish-dance.name: Cornish dance
cornish-dance.tagline: Cornish dance (Cornish: Donsyow kernewek) originates from Cornwall, UK
cornish-dance.profile: Cornish dance (Cornish: Donsyow kernewek) originates from Cornwall, UK. It has largely been shaped by the Cornish people and the industries they worked in. In most cases, particularly with the step dancing, the dances were still being performed across the region when they were collected. Cornish dance can roughly be divided into 3 areas: 'Scoot' or step dancing, 'Furry' or Feast Day dances and dance which you will often find in a 'Troyl', the Cornish equivalent of a céilidh.
cornish-dance.insight: Community or Furry Dances are hinted at from 1700 when Edward Lluyd noted that 'Elygen' (Illogan) held its 'feast or furri day the first Sunday before or after St.

el-vito.name: El vito
el-vito.tagline: Spain, 16th century — "El Vito" is a traditional folk song and dance music of Andalusia whose origins can be traced back to the 1…
el-vito.profile: "El Vito" is a traditional folk song and dance music of Andalusia whose origins can be traced back to the 16th century. Its name refers to Saint Vitus, patron of dancers. It was created in the nineteenth century as a dancing song typical of the bolero. It includes steps in the art of bullfighting and is usually played by women. The typical costume includes jacket and brimmed hat.
el-vito.insight: Folk duo Esther & Abi Ofarim recorded a version of "El Vito" for their 1967 album 2 in 3.
sources: Source: El vito on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_vito

danish-folk-dance.name: Danish folk dance
danish-folk-dance.tagline: Danish folk dance is characterized by being easy going, gentle, and relatively easy to learn
danish-folk-dance.profile: Danish folk dance is characterized by being easy going, gentle, and relatively easy to learn. Danish folk dance is mainly a social dance involving groups or groups of couples of dancers, often designed for large gatherings. The dances were supposed to be simple enough for everyone to join in. Danish folk dances are made for social and educational purposes, generally speaking not for exhibitional purposes. The canonized history of Danish folk dance highlights a performance by Philochoros in Copenhagen in 1899 with some Danish students in the audience as a triggering factor.
danish-folk-dance.insight: In 1901, some of the same students who were now students of gymnastics founded a formal organization, the Danish Association for the Promotion of Folk-Dancing (Foreningen til Folkedansens Fremme).
sources: Source: Danish folk dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_folk_dance

egg-dance.name: Egg dance
egg-dance.tagline: Germany — traditional Easter game in which eggs are laid on the ground or floor, and the goal is to dance among them,…
egg-dance.profile: An egg dance is a traditional Easter game in which eggs are laid on the ground or floor, and the goal is to dance among them, damaging as few as possible. The egg was a symbol of the rebirth of the earth in Pagan celebrations of spring, and was adopted by early Christians as a symbol of the rebirth of man at Easter. Another form of egg dancing was a springtime game depicted in the painting of Pieter Aertsen. The goal was to roll an egg out of a bowl while keeping within a circle drawn by chalk, and then flip the bowl to cover the egg.
egg-dance.insight: The event was described in an 1895 issue of The American Magazine as follows.

fandango.name: Fandango
fandango.tagline: Spain and Portugal — castanets, guitar, and a courtship danced for centuries. Manuel de Falla turned it into ballet in 1919.
fandango.profile: Fandango is a lively partner dance originating in Spain, usually in triple meter, traditionally accompanied by guitars, castanets, tambourine or hand-clapping. Fandango can both be sung and danced. Sung fandango is usually bipartite: it has an instrumental introduction followed by "variaciones". Sung fandango usually follows the structure of "cante" that consist of four or five octosyllabic verses (coplas) or musical phrases (tercios). Occasionally, the first copla is repeated. The meter of fandango is similar to that of the bolero and seguidilla.
fandango.insight: == Origins == The earliest fandango melody is found in the anonymous "Libro de diferentes cifras de guitarra" from 1705, and the earliest description of the dance itself is found in a 1712 letter by Martín Martí, a Spanish priest. In the 21st century, Italian composer Carlotta Ferrari has written several Fandangos; particularly, her 2020 "Fandango RPS" uses the Restarting Pitch Space harmony system.
sources: Source: Fandango on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fandango

dutch-folk-dance.name: Dutch folk dance
dutch-folk-dance.tagline: Germany — Dutch folk dance encompasses traditional dances that were performed by the folk
dutch-folk-dance.profile: Dutch folk dance encompasses traditional dances that were performed by the folk. While foreigners and the Dutch often associate Dutch folk dance with clog dancing, clogs actually limit the range of dance moves. Consequently, the dance is typically performed in shoes. Historically, the Dutch folk dance was part of their Church going attire, which included shoes. Clogs were reserved for work, but during harvest feasts following the harvest, farmers would dance in clogs, as they had been wearing them throughout the day.
dutch-folk-dance.insight: Dutch folk dance encompasses traditional dances that were performed by the folk.
sources: Source: Dutch folk dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_folk_dance

estonian-folk-dance.name: Estonian folk dance
estonian-folk-dance.era: Ancient circle/chain dances; systematized as 'rahvatants' early 20th c.; Dance Celebration from 1934
estonian-folk-dance.tagline: Estonia's umbrella folk-dance tradition, crowned by the Dance Celebration.
estonian-folk-dance.profile: Rahvatants is the broad umbrella of Estonian folk dance, encompassing ancient circle and chain dances, mimicry dances, set-dances, and couple dances such as the labajalavalss (flat-foot waltz, danced without rising onto the toes), kaerajaan, and tuljak (English Wikipedia; Kapper). Generally calm in character yet noted for a wide diversity of basic steps, it is typically accompanied by accordion, fiddle and other folk instruments. It is socially central to Estonian identity and concentrated in the Estonian Dance Celebration (Tantsupidu), first held in 1934 as the Dance and Gymnastic Festival within the first Estonian Games, now staged with the Song Celebration; UNESCO notes the tradition culminates in large-scale festivals every fifth year (English Wikipedia; UNESCO).
estonian-folk-dance.insight: Anna Raudkats's 1926 publication 'Eesti rahvatantsud' entrenched the idea that folk dances were old-fashioned village dances; the three most generally known - labajalavalss, kaerajaan and tuljak - are repeatedly cited as the canonical examples (Kapper, Folklore 54).

flitter-dance.name: Flitter Dance
flitter-dance.tagline: traditional dance from the Isle of Man associated with Good Friday
flitter-dance.profile: The Flitter Dance (Flitter Daunsey in Manx) is a traditional dance from the Isle of Man associated with Good Friday. It was collected by Mona Douglas in the 1940s or 50s and is popular among younger Manx dancers today.
flitter-dance.insight: A dance was collected in connection to these customs by Mona Douglas, who first mentioned it as ‘partly noted but still incomplete’ in 1937.

freilekhs.name: Freilekhs
freilekhs.tagline: Yiddish — the "happy" wedding dance. Danced immediately after the glass is broken, when joy and grief meet.
freilekhs.profile: Klezmer (Yiddish: כּלי־זמר or ,קלעזמער, romanized: klezmer) is an instrumental musical tradition of the Ashkenazi Jews of Central and Eastern Europe. The essential elements of the tradition include dance tunes, ritual melodies, and virtuosic improvisations played for listening; these would have been played at weddings and other social functions. The musical genre incorporated elements of many other musical genres including Ottoman (especially Greek and Romanian) music, Baroque music, German and Slavic folk dances, and religious Jewish music.
freilekhs.insight: The earliest written record of the use of the word was identified by Isaac Rivkind as being in a Jewish council meeting from Kraków in 1595. The first figure to collect large amounts of klezmer music was Susman Kiselgof, who made several expeditions to the Pale of Settlement from 1907 to 1915.

furiant.name: Furiant
furiant.tagline: Bohemian folk dance characterized by its rapid tempo and usage of irregular changing rhythms, hemiolas and …
furiant.profile: A furiant is a Bohemian folk dance characterized by its rapid tempo and usage of irregular changing rhythms, hemiolas and syncopation. Furiants are usually written in the time signature 34, with off-beat accents that divide their first two measures into three duple units (24). The furiant is danced in pairs. The dance became very popular in Bohemia during the 19th century, and many Czech composers such as Antonín Dvořák and Bedřich Smetana wrote furiants in their compositions.
furiant.insight: This song was first recorded by Karel Jaromír Erben in 1842,, and aided Bedřich Smetana in writing both of his furiants.

muixeranga.name: Muixeranga
muixeranga.tagline: collective name given to the performance of ancient street dances and human pyramids or castells, originati…
muixeranga.profile: The Muixeranga (Valencian: [mujʃeˈɾaŋɡa] ) is the collective name given to the performance of ancient street dances and human pyramids or castells, originating in the ancient Kingdom of Valencia (currently the Land of Valencia), which are still preserved in the town of Algemesí, 30 km (19 mi) southwest from Valencia, and certain other Valencian towns. The muixeranga is much more than an artistic acrobatic dance.
muixeranga.insight: The first solemn celebrations of the Virgin of Health happened in 1724, so this is the earliest that the muixeranga could be linked to this celebration.

furlana.name: Furlana
furlana.tagline: Italy — The furlana (also spelled furlane, forlane, friulana, forlana) is an Italian folk dance from the Italian re…
furlana.profile: The furlana (also spelled furlane, forlane, friulana, forlana) is an Italian folk dance from the Italian region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. In Friulian, furlane means Friulian, in this case Friulian Dance. In Friuli there has been a Slav minority since the Slavic settlement of the Eastern Alps, and the furlana may well have originated as a Slavonic dance.
furlana.insight: It was introduced to France by André Campra in 1697 (in L'Europe galante) and 1699 (in Le carnaval de Venise, in which the first of two furlanas serves as a dance entry for a troupe of Slavs, Armenians, and Gypsies), and it quickly became a popular theatre and social dance there.

irish-dance.name: Irish dance
irish-dance.era: Traditional; competitive stepdance codified late 19th-20th c.; globalized 1994 (Riverdance)
irish-dance.tagline: Umbrella of Irish stepdance, ceili and set dancing.
irish-dance.profile: Irish dance is a group of traditional dance forms originating in Ireland, broadly divided into social dances (ceili and set dancing) and performance/solo dances (stepdance) (Wikipedia). Modern competitive stepdance is characterized by a rigid upper body and intricate, fast footwork in soft shoes (ghillies) or hard shoes; other solo forms include sean-nos (relaxed, close-to-the-floor, improvised) and festival dance. Ceili dancing is performed by groups of 2-16 to reels, jigs and hornpipes; the 30 standardized ceili dances appear in CLRG's official handbook 'Ar Rinci Ceili.' Set dances derive from French quadrilles for four couples. Accompaniment is Irish traditional music - fiddle, bodhran, concertina, flute, whistle. The form was globally popularized by Riverdance (1994).
irish-dance.insight: Irish group dancing was particularly influenced by the French quadrille in the late 18th century - a genuine France connection, but the tradition is unambiguously Irish, so the catalog's France label is a mislabel (Wikipedia).

leventikos.name: Leventikos
leventikos.tagline: Greece — Leventikos (Greek: Λεβέντικος, Levéntikos); or Bufčansko (Macedonian: Буфчанско), also known as Litós (Λιτό…
leventikos.profile: Leventikos (Greek: Λεβέντικος, Levéntikos); or Bufčansko (Macedonian: Буфчанско), also known as Litós (Λιτός), Kucano, Nešo or Pusteno, is a dance of western Macedonia, mainly performed by Slav Macedonians and Greeks in the town of Florina, Greece and in the Resen and Bitola regions in the neighbouring North Macedonia.

hop-tu-naa.profile: Hop-tu-naa is a traditional Manx dance connected to the hop-tu-naa festivities around 31 October in the Isle of Man. It is a simple processional dance for any number of two pairs of dancers. The dance shares its name with the festivities and the music to which the dance is connected.
hop-tu-naa.insight: It is not known at what date it was collected, but it was first mentioned as having been complete and collected in the Five Manx Folk Dances published in 1936.

hornpipe.profile: The hornpipe is any of several dance forms and their associated tunes, played and danced in Great Britain and Ireland and elsewhere from the 16th century until the present day. The dance is still performed in competition. George Frideric Handel's hornpipe from Water Music is one of his most famous compositions.

lezginka.name: Lezginka
lezginka.tagline: The Caucasus — Dagestan, Chechnya, Georgia, Azerbaijan. The fast warrior dance that crosses borders.
lezginka.profile: The Lezginka (Russian: Лезгинка) is a folk dance common throughout the North Caucasus. It is named after the Lezgin people. It uses a fast 68 rhythm, and can be either a solo male or a pair dance. According to Encyclopædia Britannica: Lezginka, also spelled Lezghinka, folk dance originating among the Lezgin people of the North Caucasus. It is a male solo dance (often with a sword) and also a couple dance. The man, imitating the eagle, falls to his knees, leaps up, and dances with concise steps and strong, sharp arm and body movements.
lezginka.insight: The dance has also been adapted into classical music in Aram Khachaturian's 1942 ballet Gayane.

odzemek.name: Odzemek
odzemek.tagline: Ukraine — Slovak solo traditional dance for men, which always has an improvised character
odzemek.profile: The Odzemek (Slovak: Odzemok) is a Slovak solo traditional dance for men, which always has an improvised character. The dance starts out slow and gets faster as the dance goes on, and is traditionally danced in Slovakia and Moravian Wallachia. The name Odzemok comes from the words 'od zeme,' which means 'from the ground.' It is danced with the Valaška in most regions, but in some Eastern Slovak regions a long stick is often also used. It can be danced either solo or with a group of dancers together.
odzemek.insight: The first dance from the Slavonic Dances Op.

jig.name: Jig
jig.tagline: Spain, 16th century — The jig (Irish: port, Scottish Gaelic: port-cruinn) is a form of lively folk dance in compound metre, as we…
jig.profile: The jig (Irish: port, Scottish Gaelic: port-cruinn) is a form of lively folk dance in compound metre, as well as the accompanying dance tune. It first gained popularity across the British Isles in the 16th-century, and was adopted on mainland Europe where it eventually became the final movement of the mature Baroque dance suite (the French gigue; Italian and Spanish giga). It is most associated with Irish dance music, Scottish country dance, French Canadian traditional music and dance and the Métis people in Canada.
jig.insight: It is second in popularity only to the reel in traditional Irish dance, and in Scottish country dance jigs and reels are the two quicktime dance forms.

kolo.name: Kolo
kolo.tagline: The Slavic circle dance — opens every Serbian wedding, closes every village festival.
kolo.profile: Kolo (Serbian Cyrillic: Коло) is a South Slavic circle dance, found under this name in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, and Serbia. It is inscribed on the UNESCO List of Intangible Cultural Heritage for Serbia.
kolo.insight: UNESCO inscribed Serbia's Kolo on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2017 — recognising not just the dance but the social fabric it carries. Tradition holds that whoever joins the kolo is welcomed regardless of standing, age, or origin; the circle is intentionally non-hierarchical, and the dancer who leads (the kolovođa) is chosen by collective decision rather than rank.

karsilamas.name: Karsilamas
karsilamas.tagline: Greek-Turkish 'facing dance' in 9/8 time — the limping rhythm of the Anatolian wedding floor.
karsilamas.profile: Karsilamas (Turkish: karşılama; Greek: καρσιλαμάς) is a folk dance spread all over Northwest Turkey and carried to Greece by Anatolian Greek immigrants. The term "karşılama" means "encounter, welcoming, greeting" in Turkish. The dance is popular in Northwestern areas of Turkey, especially on wedding parties and festivals. This dance is also found in many areas of Greece, such as the Aegean islands (Syros, Kythnos, Lesvos, etc.) as well as in Thrace and Macedonia. Apart from Karsilamas, in Greece and Cyprus there is a similar dance named Antikrystos.
karsilamas.insight: Karsilamas's 9/8 time signature — the 'limping' 2+2+2+3 count — connects it to a vast Anatolian rhythmic family that includes Bulgaria's kopanitsa, Macedonia's lesnoto, and Ottoman-era court music; the same off-balance feel appears in dance forms from Albania to Armenia. Pontic Greek diaspora carried karsilamas from the Black Sea coast to Greek communities worldwide after the the early-20th-century Greek-Turkish population exchange.

sousta.name: Sousta
sousta.era: Ancient roots (linked to the Pyrrhic war-dance tradition); name from Venetian 'sousta' (carriage spring)
sousta.tagline: Cretan/Dodecanese couples courtship dance with hopping steps.
sousta.profile: A Greek folk dance performed at weddings as courtship between partners; prominent in Crete, the Dodecanese and the broader Aegean, and described as second only to the syrtos in commonness. A three-step dance with a 'hopping' bounce - two jump-steps forward, one back - with crossed-over linked hands symbolizing unity. Carries symbolism of romance and marriage; historically a socialisation rite among village youth. Music typically on Cretan or Pontian lyra (or violin), laouto, and mandolin/askomandoura. Named from the Venetian word for a carriage spring, reflecting its bouncy motion (English Wikipedia; IJESSR).
sousta.insight: The sousta exists in many officially documented island variants (Crete, Rhodes, Halki, Leros, Kalymnos, Karpathos, Kos, Tilos, Samos, Symi); on Rhodes alone scholars record distinct village forms in a peer-reviewed IJESSR study.

Dvořák's 5th, 7th and 11th Slavonic Dances are in the form of the skočná.

syrtos.name: Syrtos
syrtos.tagline: One of the oldest, most widespread Greek chain dances.
syrtos.profile: A collective name for a family of Greek folk dances; open circle/curving line, dancers link hands facing right, led by a leader who improvises and may break away. Among the most ancient Greek dances, described by Lucian (c. AD 125-190). Mainland versions (Peloponnese, Thessaly, Macedonia, Thrace) use 7/8; Crete, the Aegean, Asia Minor and Constantinople use 4/4 (slow-quick-quick). Traditionally segregated lines of men and women, the leader holding the second dancer by a handkerchief; played on regional instruments (Cretan lyra/violin, laouto, clarinet). Central to weddings and religious festivals (English Wikipedia; Britannica).
syrtos.insight: Syrtos and kalamatianos share identical steps but differ in meter (4/4 vs 7/8); the name derives from syro, 'to drag/lead' (English Wikipedia; Britannica).

schuhplattler.name: Schuhplattler
schuhplattler.era: Possible medieval roots; modern regulated form 19th c.
schuhplattler.profile: The Schuhplattler is a folk dance of the Eastern Alps (Upper Bavaria, Tyrol, Salzburg) in which men stomp, clap and strike the soles of their shoes (Schuhe), thighs and knees with flat (platt) hands. It is often a couple dance: men perform leaps and slapping sequences to the Landler portion of the music in 3/4 time (originally zither and guitar, later accordion), while women in dirndls twirl; a boys-only form (reiner Burschenplattler) also exists. The tradition is preserved by Trachtenvereine (costume clubs) in Bavaria, Austria and German-immigrant communities worldwide (English Wikipedia; Society of Folk Dance Historians).
schuhplattler.insight: Often said to mimic the courtship display of the Auerhahn (wood grouse); the modern form was popularized after locals performed it for King Maximilian II of Bavaria on 15 July 1858, and the first Schuhplattler society formed at Miesbach in 1861 (English Wikipedia).

tsifteteli.profile: A rhythm and dance of Anatolia and the Balkans, the Greek counterpart of Turkish ciftetelli (Turkish 'double-stringed,' from a violin technique). In Greece it functions as the Greek 'belly dance': a solo improvisational form with hip undulations, shoulder shimmies and sinuous arm movements, typically in 4/4 (also cited as 2/4). Performed informally at weddings, glentia and festivals, mostly initiated by women; also professionally in tavernas and bouzouki clubs. Accompanied by violin, bouzouki and percussion; common in rebetiko/laiko (English Wikipedia; Folkdance Footnotes).

The Harlem shake is commonly incorporated into the social dance Litefeet, as is the "Chicken Noodle Soup, the Tone Wop (often mistakenly named the "Toe Whop"), the Rev Up and the Aunt Jackie. Moves often include: shuffling, hat tricks, and shoe tricks.

turfing.profile: Turfing (or turf dancing) is a form of street dance that originated in Oakland, California, United States, characterized by rhythmic movement combined with waving, floor moves, gliding, flexing, and contortioning. It was developed by youth from West Oakland and organized by dancer Jeriel Bey, who coined the name "turf dancing," or "Turfin" and named his Organization The Architeckz™. Bey named the dance form as an acronym for "Taking Up Room on the Floor." The style was originally known by the terms "having fun with it" or "hitting it", but these names didn't seem marketable.

ballroom-dance.profile: Ballroom dance is a set of European partner dances enjoyed socially and competitively worldwide. Per Encyclopædia Britannica, it is a type of social dancing originally practiced in Europe and the United States, performed by couples following prescribed steps, historically distinguished from folk dance by its association with elite social classes and invitational dance events. With the rise of DanceSport the term narrowed to the dances recognized by two principal schools - the International School (Standard and Latin) and the American School (Smooth and Rhythm) (Wikipedia).
ballroom-dance.insight: Ballroom dance democratized over the 20th century from an aristocratic pastime into a global social and competitive activity, popularized by figures such as Vernon and Irene Castle, Fred Astaire, and Arthur Murray (Encyclopædia Britannica).

liscio.profile: Liscio or ballo liscio ("smooth" or "smooth dance" respectively in Italian) is a genre of music originating in the 19th century in the northern Italian region of Romagna under the influence of Viennese ballroom dances including the mazurka, waltz, polka, schottische, march. It later became popular and spread to the rest of the country. The accordion, which was also a 19th-century invention, features prominently. The tradition contrasts with older Italian folk dances in which the fiddle was the primary instrument.
liscio.insight: Raoul Casadei — bandleader of Italy's most famous liscio orchestra across six decades — produced over a thousand songs and turned ballo liscio into a national pop genre during the 1970s and 80s; his 1973 'Ciao Mare' remains the unofficial anthem of the Italian Adriatic coast, played at every sagra (village festival) from Ravenna to Rimini.

one-step.profile: The One-Step was a ballroom dance popular in social dancing at the beginning of the 20th century. Troy Kinney writes that One-Step originated from the Turkey Trot dance, with all mannerisms of the latter removed, so that "of the original 'trot' nothing remains but the basic step". The One-Step included the following basic figures (and a number of more advanced ones): The Castle Walk (invented and introduced by Mr. and Mrs. Vernon Castle). The Turn is a walking step, pivoting on one foot to change direction.

albanian-war-dances.profile: Albanian war dances (Albanian: valle luftarake) were historically performed before departure for battle and now appear at feasts and festivals, differing by region. Early-19th-century Western travellers described a circle dance around a ritual purifying fire, beginning with a battle cry and war drums; the northern-highland sword-dance type spread to the Lezha lowlands via mountain shepherds. The Rugova variant is a mock duel between two men competing for a maiden (English Wikipedia, 'Albanian war dances').
albanian-war-dances.insight: A living relic of pantomimic combat rites linking modern Albanian identity to ancient Illyrian/Pyrrhic martial traditions; the folktale 'Skanderbeg and Ballaban' narrates the sword dance performed by Skanderbeg's soldiers before battle (Robert Elsie, Albanian Folktales and Legends, via English Wikipedia).

choreia.profile: Choreia (Ancient Greek: χορεία, romanized: choreía) is a circle dance accompanied by singing (see Greek chorus, choros), in ancient Greece. Homer refers to this dance in his epic poem, the Iliad. Terms descended from Greek choreia that are used for circle dances in a number of other countries are: horon, in Turkey khorovod (хоровод), in Russia khora (хора), in Ukraine hora, in Romania and Moldova horo (хоро), in Bulgaria oro (оро), in North Macedonia and Montenegro

carol.profile: A carol is a festive song, generally religious but not necessarily connected with Christian church worship, and sometimes accompanied by a dance. A caroller (or caroler) is someone who sings carols, and is said to be carolling (or caroling). Today the carol is represented almost exclusively by the Advent carol, the Christmas carol, and to a lesser extent by the Easter carol; however, despite their present association with religion, this has not always been the case.

domkach.name: Domkach
domkach.tagline: Nagpuri wedding dance of joy and satire
domkach.profile: Domkach (or Damkach) is a folk dance of Bihar, Jharkhand and Nepal's Madhesh province, performed during wedding ceremonies; in Bihar it features in the Mithila and Bhojpur regions and in Jharkhand it is a Nagpuri folk dance (Wikipedia). The women and men of the bride's and groom's families form a semicircle holding each other's waists and dance to satirical, joyful songs accompanied by dholak and ghungroo (Wikipedia). In its classic Chotanagpur form, the women of the groom's family perform it through the night after the baraat (wedding procession) has departed, keeping themselves awake and entertained (EZCC).
domkach.insight: The dance is named after the Dambru/Dom musical instrument; Nagpuri Domkach is sub-classified into Ekharia, Dohri and Jhumta variants, and the wedding-season run extends from Deouthan in Kartik (Oct-Nov) to the Rath Yatra in Ashadh (Jun-Jul) (Wikipedia).

daychovo-horo.name: Daychovo horo
daychovo-horo.era: Originated in North Bulgaria; popularized post-WWII
daychovo-horo.tagline: Northern Bulgarian 9/8 circle dance with a calling leader.
daychovo-horo.profile: A Bulgarian folk dance in nine-beat meter (9/16 or 9/8), the Daychovo-type rhythm being 2+2+2+3. Unusual in being a circle dance that nevertheless has a leader who calls figures/variations. Traditionally danced 'na prava' (straight line) by men grasping neighbors' belts in an X, or in an open mixed circle with V handhold. Originating in North Bulgaria, accompanied by gaida, gadulka, kaval, accordion and tapan (English Wikipedia; Folk Dance Federation of California).
daychovo-horo.insight: The name means 'Daycho's dance.' Per dance researcher Boris Conev (via Dick Crum), it traces to a 19th-century Pleven cattle merchant named Daycho whose downfall after 1878 inspired derisive tavern lyrics set to a lively 9/16 melody (Folk Dance Federation of California).

conga-line.name: Conga line
conga-line.tagline: Carnival processional line dance from Cuba.
conga-line.profile: The conga line is a novelty line dance derived from the Cuban carnival conga (comparsa) of Santiago de Cuba, where neighborhood comparsas march in serpentine processions (arrollando) descended from Afro-Cuban Congolese cabildos. Dancers form a line, each holding the waist of the person ahead, with three shuffle steps and a kick on the fourth beat, to a staccato conga-drum rhythm (plus the corneta china in Santiago). It became a US craze in the 1930s-1950s, popularized by Desi Arnaz and Xavier Cugat (English Wikipedia; Harvard ReVista).
conga-line.insight: The conga was one of the earliest successful 20th-century Cuban musical exports, helping prepare international audiences for son, mambo and salsa - even as it was banned at times in Cuba as a dangerous mass gathering (English Wikipedia; Harvard ReVista).

corridinho.name: Corridinho
corridinho.tagline: Portugal — form of Portuguese folk dance, namely in the Algarve region
corridinho.profile: The corridinho is a form of Portuguese folk dance, namely in the Algarve region. The origin of the dance itself is unclear and believed older, although it gained popularity in the 1800s. The name derives from correr, to run which partly describes this type of dance. The dance was performed in a round (dança de roda) in the open air. The oldest musical instruments recorded were small flutes or fifes (pífaro) and harmonicas, (harmónica) until the accordion was implemented and dominated ever since.
corridinho.insight: The corridinho is a form of Portuguese folk dance, namely in the Algarve region.

dances-of-universal-peace.profile: The Dances of Universal Peace (DUP) are a spiritual practice that employs singing and dancing the sacred phrases of the world's religions. Their intention is to raise consciousness and promote peace between diverse religions according to one stated goal. The DUP are of North American Sufic origin. They combine chants from many world faiths with dancing, whirling, and a variety of movement with singing.
dances-of-universal-peace.insight: The very first dance took place on 16 March, 1968 in San Francisco, California.

assyrian-folk-dance.tagline: Assyrian folk dances are sets of dances that are performed throughout the world by Assyrians, mostly on occ…
assyrian-folk-dance.profile: Assyrian folk dances are sets of dances that are performed throughout the world by Assyrians, mostly on occasions such as weddings, community parties and other jubilant events. Assyrian folk dances are mainly made up of circle dances like ballet that are performed in a line, which may be straight, curved, or both. Most of the dances allow unlimited number of participants, with the exception of the Sabre Dance, which require three at most. Assyrian dances would vary from weak to strong, depending on the mood and tempo of a song.
assyrian-folk-dance.insight:
== History ==

Lily Oraham Taimoorazy, sometimes considered to be the mother of Assyrian folk dancing, founded a dance group called the Shamiram Folkloric Group in Tehran in 1957.

cachua.profile: The cachua (qachwa, qhaswa, kashua, kaswa, kachura) (ˈqɑt͡ʃwa or ˈχɑt͡ʃwa, diminutive form cachuita) is a Latin-American baroque dance form found mainly in Peru. It still exists today as a circle dance. The term comes from the Quechua language qhachwa, meaning "round dance", via Spanish. It was also applied to some villancicos to Spanish texts with cachua rhythm, such as two examples in a report submitted to Charles IV of Spain c.1788-1790. It is in rapid unsyncopated 2/4 time.

The dance is a typical Medieval dance. The dance is danced traditionally in a circle, but when there are many dancers, they usually let it swing around in various wobbles within the circle.

ganggangsullae.name: Ganggangsullae
ganggangsullae.tagline: Korean women's moonlit harvest circle dance
ganggangsullae.profile: Ganggangsullae is a seasonal harvest and fertility ritual of southwestern Korea, performed primarily at Chuseok (Korean Thanksgiving) in the eighth lunar month (UNESCO). Under the full moon, women join hands in a circle and sing and dance all night under a lead singer, with the group answering the refrain 'ganggangsullae'; during interludes they mime farm and fishing-village vignettes. Traditionally performed only by women at night without instruments, it offered a rare freedom from restrictive Joseon-era rules governing rural young women.
ganggangsullae.insight: Designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property of Korea in 1966 and inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2009, ganggangsullae is now taught in elementary-school music curricula and performed nationwide as a representative Korean folk art (UNESCO; Korea Heritage Service).

janani-jhumar.profile: Janani Jhumar also Janani Jhumair is a Nagpuri folk dance of the Chota Nagpur Plateau region of Jharkhand. It is a women centric dance. The music of instruments used, such as mandar, dhol and bansi. The women hold each other's hand, form a linear line and dance in a circle. The dance movements have feminine grace. While women sing and dance, men play musical instruments. This dance is performed in the festival of Karam and Jitiya. This dance is also called Angnai when it is done in the courtyard.

jhumair.name: Jhumair
jhumair.era: Traditional; agrarian roots in the Chota Nagpur plateau
jhumair.tagline: Sadan harvest dance of the Chota Nagpur plateau
jhumair.profile: Jhumair (Jhumar) is a folk dance of the Sadan - the Indo-Aryan ethnic groups of Chotanagpur - performed across Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Assam and West Bengal, and also by Adivasi communities, mainly associated with the harvest season (Wikipedia). Performers stand in a row or circle, hold hands, sing couplets, sway, clap and perform timed jumps, accompanied by the mandar, dhol, nagara and bansuri. Regional and stylistic varieties include Nagpuri, Khortha, Kurmali and Panchpargania Jhumar, plus the gendered Mardani (men's) and Janani (women's) Jhumar (Wikipedia; Historified).
jhumair.insight: Folk artist Mukund Nayak of Jharkhand is a celebrated exponent of Nagpuri Jhumar, having taught and recorded the form for decades to preserve its Sadan roots (Grokipedia, citing Ranchi University records).

ghost-dance.name: Ghost Dance
ghost-dance.tagline: Native American religious circle dance of renewal — NOT Chinese
ghost-dance.profile: The Ghost Dance (Caddo: Nanissáanah, also 'Ghost Dance of 1890') is a ceremony and new religious movement of Native American peoples, founded on the millenarian teachings of the Northern Paiute prophet Wovoka (Jack Wilson) in 1889 (English Wikipedia; Britannica). Based on the traditional round/circle dance, it spread across the Western United States and is associated with the 1890 Wounded Knee Massacre. There is no genuine Chinese dance by this name.
ghost-dance.insight: A profoundly significant Indigenous North American spiritual movement of cultural revitalization and resistance; it must be treated respectfully as a sacred ceremony, not entertainment (Britannica; World History Encyclopedia).

kalamatianos.name: Kalamatianos
kalamatianos.era: Roots in antiquity; modern name from the town of Kalamata
kalamatianos.profile: One of Greece's best-known dances, widely regarded as the national dance; danced in a chain/open circle, counterclockwise, dancers holding hands. Beat 7/8 subdivided 3+2+2 (slow-quick-quick); 12 steps over 4 bars (10 forward counterclockwise, 2 back). The lead dancer often holds the second by a handkerchief to perform elaborate steps and acrobatics. Inclusive (men, women, children); performed at weddings, festivals and diaspora gatherings, accompanied by clarinet, violin, laouto, drums and often bouzouki (English Wikipedia; Costa Navarino).
kalamatianos.insight: Steps are identical to the syrtos but the meter differs (kalamatianos 7/8, syrtos 4/4); the kalamatianos is on Greece's National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage (a national, not UNESCO, recognition).

halay.name: Halay
halay.tagline: Turkey's signature line dance — hands joined, davul and zurna driving the village floor.
halay.profile: Halay is the national dance of Turkey. It refers to all traditional circular and line dances performed across the country. The term is used among Turks, Kurds, Arabs, and Asia Minor Greeks (particularly Pontic Greeks, Karamanlides, and Cappadocian Greeks). Circular and line dances in Turkey are commonly performed at weddings and festive gatherings, traditionally accompanied by the zurna and davul, or sometimes by the singing of the dancers themselves. In recent years, electronic instruments have increasingly been used in place of traditional musical instruments.
halay.insight: The earliest known written definition of the word halay appears in the 1932 ethnographic compilation Anadilden Derlemeler by Hamit Zübeyir Koşay and İshak Işıtman, where halay is defined as a hand-held line dance from Central Anatolia, accompanied by the zurna and davul.
