chopi.name: Chopi (Choobi)
chopi.tagline: Gulf-style Iranian line dance led by a handkerchief-waving leader
chopi.profile: In the Iranian context, 'chopi'/'choobi' denotes a Bandari/Khaleeji-style group line dance of southern Iran, related to the broader Gulf (khaleeji) and stick-dance traditions. The word is cognate with the Lori/Lorestan collective dance 'Chopi,' in which a leader called the sarchoopi stands at the front waving one or two colored handkerchiefs while the others hold hands and synchronize their steps to a solo singer accompanied by sorna and kamancheh (orienttrips.com). It is also tied to choob/choub-bazi ('stick play'), a chain or social dance found across Iran (Choub bazi, Wikipedia).
chopi.insight: The root 'chop/choob' (stick/wood) links these Gulf and Lori forms to the trans-national Iraqi Chobi/Choubi and the Kurdish copi, all sharing the same etymology and line-dance character (Choub bazi, Wikipedia).
chopi.image_significance: The Lur handkerchief-led chain. A representative image shows a line or row formation, often with canes, swords or flowing veils — Lorestan (Lur), Iran.

zar.name: Zar
zar.era: documented in southern Iran from the 19th century (African diaspora origins)
zar.tagline: Afro-Iranian spirit-possession healing ritual of the Persian Gulf coast
zar.profile: Zar (Zar) in southern Iran is a ritual healing and spirit-negotiation practice of the Afro-Iranian communities of the Persian Gulf coast, especially Hormozgan, Bandar Abbas and Qeshm Island (Encyclopaedia Iranica). 'Bad' (wind) is the general term for possessing spirits, and 'zar' refers to the most dangerous winds - believed to come from Africa - as well as the ritual used to engage and pacify them (Project MUSE; Iranica). Led by a Baba Zar or Mama Zar, the ceremony uses drumming, incantations sung in mixed Persian, Arabic, Swahili and Indian, incense and rhythmic movement until the possessed person responds to the specific beat of their spirit (Encyclopaedia Iranica). It is a healing/adorcism practice, not entertainment.
zar.insight: The Iranian zar is part of the wider Zar cult of the Red Sea and East Africa, spread through the Indian Ocean slave trade; in DSM-IV it was listed as a culture-bound syndrome (Iranian Journal of Psychiatry, NCBI).
zar.image_significance: Spirit-possession healing ritual — not entertainment. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — S. coast, Iran.

yalli.name: Yalli
yalli.tagline: Ancient Azerbaijani collective chain dance, UNESCO-listed from Nakhchivan
yalli.profile: Yalli (Yalli) is an Azerbaijani collective circle/chain/line dance involving games, pantomime (bird and animal imitations) and physical movements, starting slowly and accelerating to near-running speed (UNESCO ICH; Halay, Wikipedia). It is performed hand-in-hand or by finger-grips, traditionally accompanied by zurna and davul (and nagara) (Halay, Wikipedia). Variants include Kochari and Tenzere; 'Yalli (Kochari, Tenzere), traditional group dances of Nakhchivan' was inscribed on 28 November 2018 at the 13th session (13.COM) of UNESCO's Intergovernmental Committee in Port Louis, Mauritius, on Azerbaijan's nomination, on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding (UNESCO ICH). It is also danced by Iranian Azerbaijanis in northwestern Iran.
yalli.insight: Though filed here under Iran, Yalli is fundamentally an Azerbaijani dance, and the UNESCO 2018 listing is Azerbaijan's (Nakhchivan), not Iran's (UNESCO ICH).
yalli.image_significance: The circle that never breaks. A representative image shows upright carriage, sweeping arm lines and embroidered dress — Nakhchivan/NW Iran, Iran/Azerbaijan.

baba-karam.name: Baba Karam
baba-karam.tagline: Playful Persian character dance mimicking the urban tough-guy
baba-karam.profile: Baba Karam is a Persian urban social/character dance performed to the song 'Baba Karam,' which dates to the Qajar dynasty (1794-1925) and was first sung by Hossein Hamedanian around 1920, later revived by Vigen Derderian; it belongs to the koocheh-bazaari / roo-hozi genre (middleeasterndancing.com). The dance portrays the jahel or luti - undereducated urban 'tough guys' living by a code of honor - using a fedora and neckerchief, posturing strut, hip sways, hand movements and expressive eyebrow and lip play (middleeasterndancing.com). Wikipedia notes Baba Karam is sometimes used as a term for contemporary Persian hip-hop dancing (Iranian dance, Wikipedia).
baba-karam.insight: It was popularized by the 'tough guy' film genre and by dancer Jamileh; whether it evolved from real jahel dancing or as a caricature remains unconfirmed (middleeasterndancing.com).
baba-karam.image_significance: Swagger of the Tehran tough-guy. A representative image shows a line or row formation, often with canes, swords or flowing veils — Tehran, Iran.

hanter-dro.name: Hanter Dro
hanter-dro.era: Traditional (declined mid-19th c.; revived in modern fest-noz)
hanter-dro.tagline: Breton Vannetais chain dance, the 'half-turn,' paired with an dro.
hanter-dro.profile: Hanter-dro (Breton, literally 'half-turn') is a Breton chain dance from the pays Vannetais (Wikipedia FR; folk sources). Unlike the 'arm dances' an dro and the ridees, it is held firmly and is a 'feet dance,' like the gavotte; dancers stand in a chain (traditionally alternating men and women) holding hands with arms held still, body turned slightly left. It derives from Renaissance branles and had become moribund by the mid-19th century, progressively supplanted by the larides that derived from it. Combined with an dro it produces the dans tricot (dans trikot); the laride de Kervignac is a particular Hanter-dro form of the Lorient/Hennebont area. It is danced in fest-noz to sung kan-ha-diskan or instrumental accompaniment.
hanter-dro.insight: Often paired/alternated with an dro within the same suite (dans tricot), it is recommended as a beginner-friendly fest-noz dance because of its simple held step (Wikipedia FR; fest-noz guides).
hanter-dro.image_significance: Half-turn of the Vannetais chain. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — Brittany (Vannetais), France.

sonderhoning.name: Sonderhoning
sonderhoning.era: Oldest tunes from the 1700s; continuous ~300-year tradition
sonderhoning.tagline: Maritime couple dance from Fano island.
sonderhoning.profile: Sonderhoning is a traditional couple dance and melody type from the village of Sonderho on the island of Fano off Denmark's west coast. The dance is a pols (a three-step turning couple dance in a circle) and is notable because the dance is in 3/4 while the melodies are most often in 2/4. It has a walking/promenade part (gangtrin) and a turning part, danced with a special hold; music is traditionally played on the fiddle, the repertoire carried for five to six generations by the Sonnichsen and Brinch families. It is the social centerpiece of Sonderho festivities, danced in traditional Fano costume (Danish Wikipedia; Fonden Gamle Sonderho; Univ. of Toronto folk-dance archive).
sonderhoning.insight: Per Fonden Gamle Sonderho, Sonderho is the only community in Denmark with a living music-and-dance tradition traceable ~300 years that never fell out of use; the foundation applied in 2018 for UNESCO listing, but it is not inscribed.
sonderhoning.image_significance: Fanø's seafaring polska in 2/4. A representative image shows the characteristic movement and dress of the tradition — Fanø, Denmark.

pravo-horo.name: Pravo Horo
pravo-horo.tagline: Bulgaria's most basic 'straight' national line dance.
pravo-horo.profile: The 'straight/right' horo, a simple village line dance in 2/4 or 6/8 (counted 3+3) with a three-measure pattern (quick-quick-slow-slow). Dancers form concentric curving lines facing in, using a hand hold or belt hold (na lesa); the basic step dives toward the center and travels counter-clockwise. Regional styles vary - smooth in Thrace, sharp with lifted knees in the Shop region, earthy in Dobrudzha (where it is called Opas). Considered the national dance of Bulgaria (English Wikipedia; Eliznik).
pravo-horo.insight: In Greek Thrace the same dance is called Zonaradiko; it is a staple of weddings and feast days and can continue for hours, the in-and-out motion becoming hypnotic (English Wikipedia).
pravo-horo.image_significance: The line dance every Bulgarian knows. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — national, Bulgaria.

paydushko-horo.name: Paydushko Horo
paydushko-horo.profile: A Balkan line dance in 5-beat meter divided 2+3 (quick-slow), particularly associated with Bulgaria and North Macedonia. Dancers face left holding hands; traditionally a men's dance, now often mixed. The basic footwork pairs 'step-hop' and 'step-step' patterns producing a characteristic limping gait. In southern Bulgaria, Macedonia and Greece the quick-slow is sometimes reversed to slow-quick (3+2) (English Wikipedia; Folkdance Footnotes).
paydushko-horo.insight: The name comes from Turkish paytak ('a person with uneven legs'); the dance is among the strongest candidates for a genuinely pan-Balkan village dance, appearing as Pajdusko, Payduska, Baidouska, Paidusca and Pajtushka across the region (English Wikipedia).
paydushko-horo.image_significance: The limping 5/16 dance. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — pan-Balkan, Bulgaria.

graovsko-horo.name: Graovsko Horo
graovsko-horo.profile: A horo from the Graovo area (around Pernik) of the Shopluk region in west-central Bulgaria, performed in 2/4 time with the sharp, small, energetic Shop styling - light, agile, knee-flexed steps that look as if dancers barely touch the ground. Danced in short lines with belt or crossed-hand hold, often to gaida and tapan, punctuated by vigorous shouts. Its step pattern is shared with Kjustendilska Rachenitsa (the same pattern in 7/8) (Society of Folk Dance Historians; Tour4Fun).
graovsko-horo.insight: Graovsko unites many archetypal Shop steps and is among the region's signature dances, performed by the Philip Kutev National Folklore Ensemble (Society of Folk Dance Historians).
graovsko-horo.image_significance: 'Knitting with the feet' Shop dance. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — Shopluk, Bulgaria.

dunavsko-horo.name: Dunavsko Horo
dunavsko-horo.tagline: Northern Bulgaria's beloved New Year's Danube line dance.
dunavsko-horo.profile: A traditional chain/line dance from the Severnyashka (Northern/Danube) region, based on a simple 6-bar pravo horo in 2/4 marching time, with many variations and quick forward/back arm movements (basic pattern: five steps forward, three back). Set to the famous brass-band composition by Diko Iliev, written 18 April 1937 while he worked in the orchestra of the 36th Infantry Kozloduy Regiment at Oryahovo (Fort Collins Folk Dance; Radio Bulgaria/BNR).
dunavsko-horo.insight: Per Radio Bulgaria/BNR (quoting Taratanci's Iva Todorova), it is 'the invisible spiritual thread that connects millions of Bulgarians' and, alongside Pravo Horo, a well-known chain-dance anthem; it is played every New Year's Eve after the national anthem (Fort Collins Folk Dance; BNR).
dunavsko-horo.image_significance: Bulgaria's New Year's Eve dance. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — Danube/Severnyashka, Bulgaria.

sborenka.name: Sborenka
sborenka.profile: A circle/line dance from the Dobrudzha region of northeastern Bulgaria, performed in 2/4 time. The name translates as 'together / a gathering.' Dobrudzhan style is moderate-tempo, danced with the body leaning slightly back, chest forward, knees bent, and prominent shoulder and arm movements that mimic agricultural work (sowing, harvesting, kneading bread) - Dobrudzha being 'the granary of Bulgaria.' Typically a mixed circle or semicircle; men also dance it as a distinct men's dance (Svet Dimitrov; Magic of Art).
sborenka.insight: It is one of the signature dances of Dobrudzha, listed alongside Raka, Opas, Tropanka and the Dobrudzhanski ruchenik in regional repertoires (Svet Dimitrov).
sborenka.image_significance: Dobrudzha's earthy 'gathering' dance. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — Dobrudzha, Bulgaria.

buchimish.name: Buchimish
buchimish.era: Traditional folk; taught internationally from the 1960s
buchimish.profile: A line/chain horo from Pazardzhik county in Western Thrace, central Bulgaria, in a complex 15/16 meter counted 2+2+2+2+3+2+2. Danced in an open circle with a front belt-hold (lesa na poyas), men typically at both ends with women in the middle. Styling is flat-footed, low and small-stepped with a constant knee-flex bounce; the figure moves side to side. Accompaniment ranges from a solo gaida (bagpipe) to a full folk band with tapan (Folk Dance Federation of California; Bulgarian folk dance, Wikipedia).
buchimish.insight: Dick Crum speculated the name came from a now-lost song mentioning hemlock; today Bulgarians class it simply as a fast Thracian dance, introduced to North America by Dennis Boxell at the 1967 University of the Pacific Folk Dance Camp (Folk Dance Federation of California).
buchimish.image_significance: Fifteen-sixteenths of pure Thrace. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — W. Thrace (Pazardzhik), Bulgaria.

yankadi-macru.name: Yankadi & Macru
yankadi-macru.tagline: Susu paired courtship/seduction dance of coastal Guinea
yankadi-macru.profile: Yankadi and Macru (Makru/Makuru) are paired Susu (Soso) dances from southwestern coastal Guinea (and northwestern Sierra Leone), collectively the 'rhythm of courtship' (Leicestershire Music; mandebala.net). The dance begins slowly with Yankadi - girls and boys face each other in two rows and dance slowly toward one another; a boy places a scarf on a girl as a symbol of love. A whistle then signals the change to the faster Macru, the rows break up and couples dance individually (Mamady Keita, A Life for the Djembe, via Leicestershire Music). 'Yankadi' is glossed as 'it is good (to be here)'.
yankadi-macru.insight: Master djembefola Famoudou Konate has quipped that 'many marriages have taken place as a result of Yankadi Makru celebrations'; the pairing is danced by Susu, Mande and Temne across Forecariah, Dubreka, Coyah, Kindia, Boffa and Boke (Djembefola forum, citing Moustapha Bangoura).
yankadi-macru.image_significance: A two-speed dance of seduction. A representative image shows drum-driven communal movement, often in a circle with vivid textiles — coastal (Susu), Guinea.

bougarabou.name: Bougarabou
bougarabou.tagline: One drummer, four drums, all night
bougarabou.profile: One drummer, four drums, all night — Bougarabou (Senegal, Casamance (Jola)). Full sourced 9-field profile in research artifact; concise schema stub pending text expansion.

dogon-mask-dance.tagline: Masks that carry souls to the afterlife
dogon-mask-dance.profile: Masks that carry souls to the afterlife — Dogon Dama (Mali, Bandiagara (Dogon)). Full sourced 9-field profile in research artifact; concise schema stub pending text expansion.

maringa.name: Maringa
maringa.tagline: Bakongo couple-dance that grew into Congolese rumba
maringa.profile: Maringa was a Bakongo partnered couple-dance and music style of the former Kingdom of Loango (spanning today's Republic of the Congo, southern Gabon and Angola's Cabinda) that flourished in the bar-dancing culture of Brazzaville and Leopoldville in the 1920s-1940s. According to Wikipedia's 'Music of the Democratic Republic of the Congo', early maringa used a likembe (lamellophone), a glass bottle struck as a triangle and the patenge frame drum, with dancers swaying the hips and shifting weight from leg to leg; per Wikipedia's 'Congolese rumba', imported Cuban son records transformed maringa into Congolese rumba during the mid-1940s and 1950s.
maringa.insight: Maringa is the direct ancestor of Congolese rumba - which UNESCO inscribed in 2021 (16.COM, decided 14 December 2021) - making it a foundational root of soukous, ndombolo and much of modern African popular dance (Wikipedia; UNESCO).
maringa.image_significance: The hip-sway that became rumba. A representative image shows drum-driven communal movement, often in a circle with vivid textiles — Lower Congo (Bakongo), Congo/Angola.

mukuji.name: Mukudj
mukuji.tagline: Punu white-mask stilt dance honoring female ancestors
mukuji.profile: Mukudj (also okuyi, mokuyi, mukudji) is the masquerade dance of the Punu (Bapunu) people of southern Gabon's Ngounie and Nyanga river region, performed with white kaolin-coated masks depicting idealized female ancestral faces (Punu-Lumbo mask, Wikipedia; Metropolitan Museum). Masks are crafted and danced by male members of the Mwiri men's society. Virtuosic male dancers wear the mask atop tall stilts, dressed in raffia and skins, executing acrobatic choreography at funerals, births, initiations and other major events to invoke ancestral approval (Met Museum). The white color, from riverbed kaolin, symbolizes beauty, the afterlife and the spirits of the dead; diamond and square scarification motifs evoke Punu women and the people's nine primordial clans.
mukuji.insight: Punu white masks were among the first African artworks to win recognition from early-20th-century European modern artists, who wrongly speculated about Asian influence though the form is indigenous to southern Gabon (Metropolitan Museum); masks are treated respectfully as ancestral spirit objects.

kalela.profile: Smart suits, satirical songs — Kalela (Zambia, Luapula/Copperbelt). Full sourced 9-field profile in research artifact; concise schema stub pending text expansion.

ojapali.name: Ojapali
ojapali.tagline: Assamese narrative song-and-dance led by an oja and chorus
ojapali.profile: Ojapali is an Assamese narrative song-dance tradition performed by an ensemble led by an 'oja' (lead) supported by 'pali' (chorus), blending sung narration, dialogue, gesture and semi-improvised dramatisation, accompanied mainly by small cymbals (khutitaal) (Wikipedia). Scholars trace its roots to the pan-Indian kathakata (epic storytelling) tradition, dating its development well before Assam's neo-Vaishnavite movement; Darrang district (Mangaldai, Sipajhar) is considered a historical hub, patronised under King Dharmanarayana (1615-1637) (Wikipedia). Its strands include epic-based forms (Assamese Ramayana and Mahabharata) and Sukananni/Maroi Goa Ojapali rooted in Shakta (Shakti) worship, with Vyah Goa Ojapali belonging to the Vaishnava cult (Wikipedia; Gkseries).
ojapali.insight: Ojapali is widely regarded as a precursor that influenced Srimanta Sankaradeva's theatrical idiom (Ankiya Naat/Bhaona) and Sattriya dance; the Sangeet Natak Akademi has recognised exponents such as Lalit Chandra Nath (Award 1983) and Kinaram Nath Oja (Award 2012, Suknani Ojapali) (Wikipedia; Sangeet Natak Akademi).
ojapali.image_significance: Assam's oldest narrative song-dance. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Assam (Darrang), India.

deodhani.name: Deodhani
deodhani.era: Traditional; tied to Manasa and Kamakhya worship
deodhani.tagline: Assamese trance dance of the serpent goddess Manasa
deodhani.profile: Deodhani is a ritual trance-dance of Assam associated with the worship of the serpent goddess Manasa and the goddess Kamakhya (AssamInfo). The word means 'a woman possessed by a deity'; female deodhanis (and, at the Kamakhya temple, male deodhas) enter possession states believed to channel the goddess, dancing vigorously with rapid head rotations, open flowing hair and serpent-like movements to the beat of drums, often enacting Behula's dance from the Manasa legend. It is performed during the Deodhani/Manasa Puja festival, especially the three-day festival at Kamakhya in August, and in Than rituals in Kamrup, Darrang and Sonitpur (Burley 2019; AssamInfo).
deodhani.insight: Scholar Mikel Burley's peer-reviewed study (Religions of South Asia, 2019) documents the Kamakhya 'Dance of the Deodhas', noting devotees' claims that performers are possessed by several ferocious goddesses amid blood sacrifice (White Rose Research Online).
deodhani.image_significance: Trance dance of the snake goddess. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Assam (Bodo-Kachari), India.

ponung.name: Ponung
ponung.tagline: Adi women's circle dance led by a singing Miri
ponung.profile: Ponung is the most iconic folk dance of the Adi people of Arunachal Pradesh, performed exclusively by women (typically unmarried girls) in vibrant traditional attire during the Solung harvest festival and other auspicious occasions (Wikipedia, Adi people; MyGov). The women form a circle, sometimes holding hands, moving in slow, graceful rhythmic steps, while a single male leader called the Miri stands at the centre singing folk songs that narrate the origin of crops, the history of the Adis and creation myths (auchitya; MyGov). The Miri also plays the Yoksha, a sword-shaped instrument with loosely attached iron discs that produce a rattling sound (auchitya; North East PSC).
ponung.insight: Solung derives from 'Eso' (mithun) and 'lung' (herd), and the Ponung dances are performed on its final days alongside the exchange of meat and gifts; the women's costume includes the Gale skirt, Galuk blouse and ornaments such as the Gol Pota, Madoli and Tampilang (Wikipedia, Adi people; MyGov).
ponung.image_significance: The Adi women's harvest myth-circle. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Arunachal (Adi), India.

dhol-cholom.name: Dhol Cholom
dhol-cholom.tagline: Manipuri drum dance of the Yaoshang spring festival
dhol-cholom.profile: Dhol Cholom is a Manipuri (Meitei) drum dance of the Manipur valley performed during the Yaoshang festival (Manipuri Holi, in spring) and within the Lai Haraoba and Sankirtana traditions (Manipuri dance, Wikipedia). A group of male dancers sing and dance to the accompaniment of the dhol, a large drum used on religious occasions; the drumming builds gradually from soft to thunderous as the dance tempo intensifies, with acrobatic movement. In the classical Manipuri dance system, Dhol Cholom (with Duff Cholom) is grouped among the Shaiva (tandava) cholom dances.
dhol-cholom.insight: Dhol Cholom has no standalone English Wikipedia article; it is documented within the broader 'Manipuri dance' tradition as one of the cholom (drum/cymbal) dances alongside Pung Cholom and Kartal Cholom.
dhol-cholom.image_significance: The thunder-drum dance of Manipur. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Manipur (Meitei), India.

khuallam.name: Khuallam
khuallam.tagline: Mizo 'dance of the guests' performed at Khuangchawi
khuallam.profile: Khuallam (Khual Lam) means 'dance of the guests' in Mizo (khual = guest, lam = dance) and is performed during the Khuangchawi ceremony, a community feast hosted by those seeking the prestigious 'Thangchhuah' title (Mizoram Government; Wikipedia, Khual Lam). Guests invited from neighbouring villages enter the venue dancing, wrapping the handwoven Mizo cloth 'Puandum' over their shoulders and swaying it as they move (Wikipedia). Distinctively, no song is sung; the dance is accompanied only by traditional instruments - chiefly gongs (dar/darbu) and the khuang drum - usually in a 7/8 beat (Wikipedia; Mizoram Government).
khuallam.insight: Rooted in the pre-Christian Mizo belief system, the Khuangchawi feast and its dances were one of the routes to Pialral (paradise) via the Thangchhuah title, linking Khuallam to the social and spiritual aspiration structures of traditional Mizo society (Wikipedia, Mizo culture).
khuallam.image_significance: The dance of the guests. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Mizoram, India.

chang-lo.name: Chang Lo (Sua Lua)
chang-lo.tagline: Chang Naga victory dance of the Poanglem festival
chang-lo.profile: Chang Lo, also called Sua Lua, is a traditional folk dance of the Chang Naga tribe of Nagaland, historically performed to celebrate victory over enemies and now staged during the three-day Poanglem (Naknyulem) festival marking the harvest season (Details of India; Nagaland GK). Male dancers wear Naga warrior attire while women wear colourful traditional costumes; the dance is performed in a group with drummers, chanting, clapping and warrior-like movements, sometimes incorporating dramatic enactment. It celebrates good health, prosperity and communal unity (Details of India; TrvMe).
chang-lo.insight: No standalone English Wikipedia article exists for Chang Lo; it is documented in tribal-culture compendia and Nagaland cultural resources, consistently linked to the Chang tribe's Poanglem/Naknyulem festival.
chang-lo.image_significance: The Chang warriors' victory dance. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Nagaland (Chang), India.

hozagiri.name: Hozagiri
hozagiri.tagline: Dancing on a pitcher, lamp on the head
hozagiri.profile: Dancing on a pitcher, lamp on the head — Hozagiri (India, Tripura (Reang)). Full sourced 9-field profile in research artifact; concise schema stub pending text expansion.
hozagiri.image_significance: Dancing on a pitcher, lamp on the head. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Tripura (Reang), India.

garia.name: Garia
garia.tagline: Tripuri sowing-season dance praying for a good harvest
garia.profile: Garia (or Goria) is a folk dance of the Tripuri and Jamatia tribes of Tripura, performed during the Garia Puja festival in April that marks the commencement of the jhum (shifting cultivation) sowing season (Wikipedia, Dances of Tripura; Tripura State Portal). The festival begins with the worship of Lord Garia (Baba Garia), the deity of livestock and wealth, by the Ochai (tribal priest), followed by dancing by both men and women from village to village in a gradually increasing tempo, with mudras that mimic agricultural and natural movements (Wikipedia; Adivasi Lives Matter). It is accompanied by drums, the bamboo flute, sarinda and bamboo cymbals; celebrations continue for about seven days (Wikipedia).
garia.insight: A bamboo pole symbolising Lord Garia is worshipped with flowers and garlands; offerings include cotton thread, rice, fowl, eggs and rice beer, and during the festival no one may cross the shadow of the symbolic deity for fear of angering him (Indian Holiday; Tripura Tourism).
garia.image_significance: The sowing-season prayer dance. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Tripura (Tripuri), India.

lebang-boomani.name: Lebang Boomani
lebang-boomani.tagline: Tripuri harvest dance mimicking the catching of lebang insects
lebang-boomani.profile: Lebang Boomani (Lebang Bumani) is a harvest folk dance of the Tripuri people, performed after the Garia Puja sowing season when colourful 'lebang' insects (green cicadas) visit the hill slopes in search of sown seeds (Wikipedia, Lebang Boomani dance; Tripura State Portal). Men set the rhythm with bamboo clappers called 'tokkas,' whose sound is believed to draw the insects from hiding, while women in groups run across the slopes to catch them; the dance is a stylised re-enactment of this activity (Adivasi Lives Matter; Tripura State Portal). It is accompanied by the bamboo flute, khamb, sarinda and bamboo cymbals, and women adorn themselves with silver chains and bronze ear and nose ornaments (Tripura State Portal).
lebang-boomani.insight: The number of insects caught is traditionally believed to foretell how good the harvest will be - embedding agrarian augury in the choreography and reflecting the deep cultural life that developed around jhum cultivation (Adivasi Lives Matter; Dances of Tripura).
lebang-boomani.image_significance: The insect-catching harvest dance. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Tripura (Tripuri), India.

shad-suk-mynsiem.name: Shad Suk Mynsiem
shad-suk-mynsiem.tagline: Khasi 'Dance of the Joyful Heart' welcoming spring
shad-suk-mynsiem.profile: Ka Shad Suk Mynsiem ('Dance of the Joyful Heart/Souls') is a three-day Khasi thanksgiving spring festival held in April, marking the end of the harvest and the sowing of new seeds (Meghalaya House Delhi; Auchitya). Organised by the Seng Khasi, it centres on the historic Weiking Ground at Jaiaw, Shillong; unmarried maidens dance in an inner circle holding a white handkerchief symbolising maidenhood, while men dance vigorously around them with a sword in the right hand and a white yak-hair whisk in the left, to the beat of drums and the tangmuri pipes (Shillong Online; Sentinel Assam). The dance formation - women flanked and protected by men - reflects Meghalaya's matrilineal society (Scale Indigo).
shad-suk-mynsiem.insight: The first official Shad Suk Mynsiem dance was held on 14-15 April 1911 at Madan Weiking, Mawkhar, Shillong, and was formally given the name 'Ka Shad Suk Mynsiem' in 1912; the 2026 (115th) edition concluded in April 2026 with over a thousand dancers (The Shillong Times; Sentinel Assam).
shad-suk-mynsiem.image_significance: Dance of the Joyful Hearts. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Meghalaya (Khasi), India.

nongkrem.name: Nongkrem
nongkrem.tagline: Five-day Khasi thanksgiving dance for harvest and prosperity
nongkrem.profile: Ka Pomblang Nongkrem, popularly the Nongkrem dance, is a five-day Khasi religious festival held in autumn at Smit, headquarters of the Syiem (chief) of Hima Khyrim, about 11 km from Shillong (Government of Meghalaya). It is performed to appease the goddess Ka Blei Synshar for a bumper harvest and the prosperity of the people; the Syiem of Khyrim and the high priest conduct the Pomblang ceremony, which includes the sacrifice of goats and offering of a cock to Lei Shyllong, the god of Shillong peak (Government of Meghalaya). Unmarried maidens in fine costumes dance in an inner circle (Ka Shad Kynthei) while men dance more vigorously around them (Ka Shad Mastieh), holding a sword in the right hand and a white yak-hair whisk in the left, to the beat of drums and tangmuri pipes (Government of Meghalaya; HONEI).
nongkrem.insight: The dances take place inside the Iing Sad, a large nail-free palace of bamboo and thatch; as a living religious ceremony rather than a tourist show, visitors are asked to remain silent and stay outside the defined ritual space (Meghalaya Cabs; Government of Meghalaya).
aliases: Ka Shad Kynthei / Ka Shad Mastieh
nongkrem.image_significance: Royal goat-sacrifice thanksgiving dance. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Meghalaya (Khasi), India.

maruni.name: Maruni
maruni.tagline: One of the oldest Nepali/Gorkha festival dances
maruni.profile: Maruni is one of the oldest and most popular Nepali (Gorkha) folk dances, practised in Nepal and among Nepali-speaking communities of Darjeeling, Sikkim, Assam, Bhutan and Myanmar, performed especially during Tihar and Dashain (Wikipedia). Its choreographic origin is traditionally linked to the army of King Balihang (14th century); dancers wear colourful clothes, rich ornaments and nose rings, accompanied by the nine-instrument Naumati Baja, with the madal (maadal) drum predominating (Wikipedia; Farsight Nepal). The troupe characteristically includes a male jester/prankster figure called the 'Dhatu Waray' who provides comic relief; variants include Maruni, Thale Maruni and Sorathi (Wikipedia).
maruni.insight: Historically danced by men (including male performers cross-dressing as women), Maruni functions as a communal festival dance that knits together Nepali-Gorkha identity across the eastern Himalaya, sustained today by community and diaspora performance (Farsight Nepal; Darjeeling History Club).
maruni.image_significance: The oldest Nepali festive dance. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Nepali community, India/Nepal.

bagha-nacha.name: Bagha Nacha (Tiger dance)
bagha-nacha.era: Traditional; performance lineage cited to late 18th century
bagha-nacha.tagline: Striped tiger dancers appease the goddess in Ganjam
bagha-nacha.profile: Bagha Nacha (Tiger Dance) is a folk dance of Odisha performed in Binka and Sonepur (Subarnapur district), Berhampur and parts of Ganjam district, chiefly in the month of Chaitra (March-April) (Wikipedia). Male dancers paint themselves as tigers - a process taking three to four hours and at least two assistants - and dance to dhampa/changu drumbeats as homage to goddess Maa Budhi Thakurani, whose vahana is the tiger. Performers are not necessarily professional dancers; they train two to four weeks under a mentor. Four changus are required, and devotees observe vows, fasting and celibacy (Wikipedia; Hindu Blog).
bagha-nacha.insight: In January 2025 more than 40 male dancers performed Bagha Nacha in the Republic Day parade ensemble organised by the Ministry of Culture, and an Odia feature film on the tradition was released the same month (Wikipedia).
bagha-nacha.image_significance: Odisha's tiger dance of devotion. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Odisha (Ganjam), India.

ghumra.name: Ghumura
ghumra.tagline: Kalahandi's heroic pot-drum war dance of Odisha
ghumra.profile: Ghumura (Ghumra) is a folk dance of the Kalahandi district of western Odisha, named after the ghumura - a pitcher-shaped earthen kettle-drum tied to the dancer's neck whose face is traditionally covered with monitor-lizard skin (Wikipedia; Swadesi). Classed as folk though its mudras carry classical resemblance, it began as a 'Veera Vadya' war dance used to embolden soldiers and is now performed during Nuakhai and Dussehra. It is male-oriented, performed in lines or geometric formations by 15-40 dancers, accompanied by nishan, dhol, taal and madal, and linked in myth to the Chandi Purana account of Durga's battle against Mahishasura (Wikipedia; IJHSSI).
ghumra.insight: Ghumura has represented India at international events; about 100 dancers from Bhawanipatna performed it at the Republic Day Parade in New Delhi on 26 January 1999, and troupes performed at the Bharat Utsav in Moscow in July 2025 (Grokipedia, citing event records).
ghumra.image_significance: Kalahandi's warrior pot-drum dance. A representative image shows ornate costume and expressive hand-gesture (mudra) detail — Odisha (Kalahandi), India.

karma.name: Karma Naach
karma.tagline: Tribal Karam-tree worship dance of fate and harvest
karma.profile: Karma Naach (Karma dance) is a tribal folk dance of central and eastern India performed annually during the Karam (Karma) festival, in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal (Wikipedia; Prepp). Performed by communities including the Oraon, Munda, Ho, Santhal, Baiga and Gond, dancers form circles around a freshly cut branch of the sacred Karam tree (Nauclea parvifolia), arms around each other's waists, to worship Karam Devta/Karam-sani Devi - the deity of fate, fertility, youth and prosperity - seeking a good harvest. The festival falls on the 11th day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada (August-September) (Historified; Karma Naach Wikipedia).
karma.insight: The largest Karma Naach dance, with 3,049 participants forming 61 circles of 50, was achieved by the District Administration Mandla in Madhya Pradesh on 11 April 2016, recognized by Guinness World Records.
karma.image_significance: The dance of the fate-god's tree. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — central/eastern tribal, India.

lusheng-dance.name: Lusheng Dance
lusheng-dance.tagline: Miao dancers circle to reed-pipe lusheng music
lusheng-dance.profile: The Lusheng Dance is a Miao folk dance performed to the lusheng, a multi-pipe bamboo reed-mouth-organ, central to the Lusheng Festival of Qiandongnan, Guizhou (China Travel; eGuizhou government). Men play groups of lusheng while women in silver-decorated costumes dance in concentric circles; the dance also serves as courtship. It is shared by Dong, Zhuang, Yao and Bouyei peoples (CGTN).
lusheng-dance.insight: The lusheng and its dance are the defining cultural symbol of the Miao, evolving from ancient agricultural sacrifice into the grandest Miao festival celebration (China Travel; eGuizhou).
lusheng-dance.image_significance: Dance and play the reed-pipe at once. A representative image shows precise formation with fans, sleeves or masks and refined stagecraft — Guizhou (Miao), China.

bowl-dance.name: Bowl Dance
bowl-dance.era: traced to Yuan dynasty folk dance
bowl-dance.tagline: Mongolian women dancing while balancing stacked bowls
bowl-dance.profile: The Mongolian Bowl Dance (頂碗舞, ding wan wu) is a female folk dance of Inner Mongolia in which dancers balance bowls (often of milk tea) on the head while dancing with billowing arm movements, snapping wrists and shoulder shakes (Shen Yun; China Culture). It descends from Yuan-dynasty folk dance traditions and represents a ceremonial offering of milk tea to heaven, homeland and guests (HKU CCCH project; Shen Yun).
bowl-dance.insight: The dance embodies Mongolian pastoral hospitality and the steppe aesthetic of strong shoulder and wrist work, and is one of the best-known female dances of Inner Mongolia (China Culture, China Daily).
bowl-dance.image_significance: Balancing bowls on the head, dancing the steppe. A representative image shows precise formation with fans, sleeves or masks and refined stagecraft — Inner Mongolia, China.

long-drum-dance.name: Long Drum Dance
long-drum-dance.tagline: Yao dancers leap with meter-long waist drums
long-drum-dance.profile: The Long Drum Dance (長鼓舞, Changgu) is a folk dance of the Yao people popular in Guangdong, Guangxi, Hunan and other Yao areas, performed at festivals, harvests and weddings (TravelChina). Dancers wear and beat a drum about a meter (roughly 4 chi) long, performing vigorous, acrobatic movements imitating climbing, building houses and fighting tigers. It is rooted in the Yao ritual sacrifice to King Pan (Panhu).
long-drum-dance.insight: Yao Changgu was inscribed on China's second batch of national intangible cultural heritage in 2008 and inspired the famous orchestral composition 'Dance of the Yao People' (1952) (English Wikipedia; dotdotnews).
long-drum-dance.image_significance: Two long drums, one name. A representative image shows precise formation with fans, sleeves or masks and refined stagecraft — Yanbian/Yao, China.

abakua.name: Abakua
abakua.tagline: Afro-Cuban men's secret society with masked ireme dancers.
abakua.profile: Abakua is an all-male Afro-Cuban initiatory religious fraternity founded in 1836 in Regla, derived from the Ekpe ('leopard') societies of the Efik/Efut peoples of the Cross River basin (Calabar). Concentrated in Havana, Matanzas and Cardenas, organized into lodges (potencias). The masked ireme (naango, 'diablito') dancer represents an ancestral spirit, performing sharp, angular, staccato movements echoing the ekue/bonko drums; ceremonies (plantes) involve drumming, dancing and chanting in a secret Abakua language. Public appearances occur on the Day of the Three Kings (6 January) (English Wikipedia; The Appendix).
abakua.insight: Abakua is considered the only African-origin male initiatory society reconstituted in the Americas, and its rhythms profoundly influenced Cuban popular music, especially the rumba columbia (English Wikipedia).
abakua.image_significance: Cuba's only masked secret-society dance. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Calabar origin, Cuba.

tambu.name: Tambu
tambu.tagline: The 'Curacao blues' - Afro-Curacaoan drum, song and dance
tambu.profile: Tambu is the Afro-Curacaoan drum, song and dance complex, sometimes called 'the Curacao blues,' that emerged among enslaved Africans (largely from the Kongo/Angola region) under Dutch rule from the early 17th century. Per Wikipedia and ethnomusicologist Nanette de Jong, it centres on the tambu barrel drum and the chapi (hoe blade) struck as iron percussion, with call-and-response singing between a kantado and chorus over a 12/8 pulse. The accompanying dance is earthy and hip-driven yet governed by strict etiquette forbidding partners to touch; it was long banned by the Catholic Church and colonial government.
tambu.insight: Tambu is a vessel of Afro-Curacaoan memory and resistance - repressed for centuries by the Church and 1930s permit laws, it survives as a core expression of identity (Indiana University Press / Nanette de Jong; Wikipedia).
tambu.image_significance: The Curacao blues; hips that defied the ban. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Curacao.

guragigna.tagline: Same as the Gurage dance - fast, full-body, acrobatic
guragigna.profile: Guragigna is the dance of the Gurage people of Ethiopia, named after the Gurage language/people; it is the same tradition catalogued as 'Gurage dance.' Per Universal Tongue and the Mocha Ethiopia Dance Group, it features fast-paced, acrobatic, full-body movement - arms and legs swinging forward and back while jumping on alternate legs - performed at weddings, religious festivals and gatherings to masenqo and kebero. Women dance in trousers with hair covered to manage the rapid tempo.
guragigna.insight: Guragigna showcases the Gurage's athletic dance style and is a lively expression of community identity within Ethiopia's diverse dance landscape (Universal Tongue; Mocha Ethiopia Dance Group).
guragigna.image_significance: Gurage's lively footwork dance. A representative image shows drum-driven communal movement, often in a circle with vivid textiles — Gurage, Ethiopia.

mohobelo.name: Mohobelo
mohobelo.tagline: Basotho men's vigorous striding, sliding and leaping dance
mohobelo.profile: Mohobelo is the vigorous men's dance of the Basotho of Lesotho, a 'stride, slide and leap' dance marked by high kicks and acrobatic leaps (Music In Africa). Per Music In Africa, in the late 1800s Basotho men guarding outposts in the Maluti Mountains began to add energetic movements and a new style of dancing music, mohobelo, was born in the community of Ha-Molapo in the northern district of Leribe. The music follows a call-and-response pattern in a five-tone scale, the humming 'ho hoba' giving the dance its name; it requires great energy and endurance and is danced mainly in the evening for entertainment (Music In Africa; South Africa Online).
mohobelo.insight: Mohobelo travelled to South Africa's gold mines with Basotho migrant labourers in the early 20th century, where inter-mine dance contests produced the European-style brogues-and-bell-bottoms costume still seen at festivals today (Music In Africa).
mohobelo.image_significance: The Basotho men's striding/leaping dance. A representative image shows drum-driven communal movement, often in a circle with vivid textiles — Basotho, Lesotho.

pentozali.name: Pentozali
pentozali.era: 18th c. (music credited to Cretan violinist Stefanos Triantafillakis, c. 1770-1771)
pentozali.tagline: Fast Cretan war dance of high leaps and improvisation.
pentozali.profile: The trademark folk dance of Crete; a vigorous war dance with high jumping movements and improvisation. Name from pente ('five') + zalos ('step/jump') - 'five-steps,' the dance having ten steps; also punned with zali ('dizziness'). Dancers form an incomplete counterclockwise circle, arms on shoulders; the lead dancer improvises acrobatic leaps while the second holds his hand as a stable base. Starts moderate and accelerates. Instrumental music: the melody on Cretan lyra (or violin) with percussive laouto accompaniment; the lyra player directs the dance's flow (English Wikipedia; Music of Crete).
pentozali.insight: Tradition links pentozali to Cretan uprisings against the Ottomans - said to symbolize the 'fifth attempt' to liberate Crete; the music is credited to Stefanos Triantafillakis around 1770-1771 (English Wikipedia).
pentozali.image_significance: Crete's dizzying warrior dance. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — Crete, Greece.

gaga-rd.name: Gaga
gaga-rd.era: 20th c. in DR (derived from Haitian Rara via sugar-labor migration)
gaga-rd.tagline: Afro-Dominican Holy Week procession, the local form of Haitian Rara.
gaga-rd.profile: Gaga (Haitian Rara, creolized to gaga in the DR) is an Afro-Dominican religious procession of music and dance performed during Semana Santa (Holy Week) in the sugar bateyes, especially the east/southeast (San Pedro de Macoris, La Romana) and border provinces. It blends Vodu Dominicano (Las 21 Divisiones), folk Catholicism and African elements. Bands parade led by a 'dueno,' with male dancers fronting, then female dancers, then musicians; processions stop at crossroads for rituals. Instruments include futubas/vaksin (bamboo trumpets), improvised tin trumpets, palos (drums), guiras, maracas, whistles and whips (Smithsonian Folkways; Univ. of Maryland dissertation).
gaga-rd.insight: Ethnomusicologist June Rosenberg characterized Gaga as distinctively Dominican rather than Haitian even though it derives from Haitian Rara, reflecting how the batey context produced an independent Creole identity (Univ. of Maryland dissertation, Hernandez-Sang).
gaga-rd.image_significance: Haitian-rooted Lenten processional. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — batey, Dominican Republic.

palo-rd.name: Palo (Baile de palo)
palo-rd.era: Colonial roots (16th c.); continuous folk-religious practice
palo-rd.tagline: Afro-Dominican sacred drum-and-dance for saints and misterios.
palo-rd.profile: Palo (also atabales; baile de palos as the dance) is Afro-Dominican sacred drum-and-dance music with roots in the Kongo region of Central-West Africa, played at religious ceremonies coinciding with saints' days (velaciones), funerals and special occasions. Drums called palos are hollowed logs with cowhide heads: a master drum (palo mayor) with two or three slimmer alcahuetes, plus guira. Palos are tied to Dominican folk Catholicism and the cofradias, with a pantheon of misterios shared with Vodu Dominicano (Las 21 Divisiones). The baile de palos is a couple dance of 'respect,' traditionally danced unembraced; spirit possession may occur (English Wikipedia; Mediatheque Caraibe/Lameca).
palo-rd.insight: Ethnomusicologists Josue Santana and Edis Sanchez note the palos drums are considered sacred and are even 'baptized' before use - underscoring that this is a religious, not merely recreational, tradition.
palo-rd.image_significance: Sacred long-drum dance of respect. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Dominican Republic.

pripri.name: Pripri
pripri.tagline: Afro-Dominican accordion-and-balsie dance of the south/east.
pripri.profile: Pri-pri (pripri) is an Afro-Dominican music-and-dance genre built on three instruments: the one-row diatonic accordion, the guira, and the balsie (a single-headed drum whose player alters pitch with foot pressure). Danced in couples, it is markedly distinct from Cibao merengue: its rhythm is often in 12/8 rather than 4/4. In Villa Mella it is connected to the festivities of the Holy Spirit and the funerary rites of the Cofradia del Espiritu Santo, as well as secular parties. Some researchers group carabine, mangulina and guarapo within a broader 'pri-pri complex' (Ojala.do; Hoy/Museo del Hombre Dominicano).
pripri.insight: Musician-researcher Tone Vicioso calls pri-pri 'una joya' and notes Marta Ellen Davis's finding that Trujillo rejected pri-pri as too lascivious, championing merengue instead as political propaganda - explaining why pri-pri remained marginal.
pripri.image_significance: The Dominican juba/balsié complex. A representative image shows percussive hip-and-foot movement in bright street or yard settings — east/southwest, Dominican Republic.

yuka.name: Yuka
yuka.tagline: Cuban-Congo (Bantu) secular drum-dance, ancestor of rumba.
yuka.profile: Yuka is a secular Afro-Cuban tradition of drumming, singing and dancing developed in western Cuba (Matanzas, Pinar del Rio) by enslaved Kongo (Bantu) people during colonial times. The Bantu word yuka means 'to beat' and also names the three drums used (caja, mula, and the smallest). The secular couple dance is a stylized courtship contest - the man pursues, the woman avoids - featuring the vacunao pelvic thrust and movements imitating roosters and hens. Yuka predates rumba and gave rise to the yambu style; it survives in Kongo communities of Pinar del Rio (English Wikipedia).
yuka.insight: Yuka (with Abakua) is one of the principal African roots of Cuban rumba, and its drums are considered direct ancestors of the conga/tumbadora (English Wikipedia).
yuka.image_significance: A Kongo rumba antecedent. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Cuba.

yemaya-dance.name: Yemaya dance
yemaya-dance.tagline: Orisha dance honoring Yemaya, goddess of the sea.
yemaya-dance.profile: The Yemaya dance is the Afro-Cuban orisha dance for Yemaya (Yemoja), the Yoruba/Lucumi orisha of the sea and motherhood (syncretized with Our Lady of Regla; color blue), within Santeria/Regla de Ocha ritual and its staged folkloric form. It is performed to bata-drum toques (Yemaya's flowing 6/8) with akpwon/coro call-and-response in Lucumi; the dancer's arms and skirt mimic crashing waves and ocean swells in sweeping, undulating, circular motions, sometimes imitating swimming or diving. Staged by ensembles such as the Conjunto Folklorico Nacional de Cuba (Hakai Magazine; Dancing the Orishas).
yemaya-dance.insight: As scholars note, while Yemaya is honored through dance within Santeria ceremony, Yemaya is not a dance in itself - it is an orisha, and the dance is one component of orisha worship and possession ritual (Hakai Magazine).
yemaya-dance.image_significance: Orisha dance of the sea-mother. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Santeria, Cuba.

porro.name: Porro
porro.tagline: Caribbean brass-band dance music of the savannas.
porro.profile: A festive couples dance-music of Colombia's Caribbean savannas (Cordoba, Sucre, Bolivar), in 2/2 'compas partido,' derived from traditional gaita ensembles meeting European-style wind/military bands (Wikipedia ES; ColombiaOne). Two folk types: porro palitiao (Sinu River/San Pelayo) and porro tapao/sabanero (El Carmen de Bolivar). Played by 'pelayera' brass bands; popularized in orchestral form by Lucho Bermudez and Pacho Galan.
porro.insight: Ley 2259 de 2022 (19 July 2022), Art. 1: 'Reconozcase al Porro como manifestacion del Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial y el Festival del Porro de San Pelayo como una accion de salvaguardia' (SUIN-Juriscol).
porro.image_significance: The savanna brass-band dance. A representative image shows colorful regional costume and lively partner or troupe footwork — Cordoba/Sucre, Colombia.

sanjuanero.name: Sanjuanero
sanjuanero.profile: A festive Colombian bambuco of Huila/Tolima tied to the San Pedro/San Juan festivities; the music was composed in 1936 by Anselmo Duran Plazas with lyrics by Sofia Gaitan Yanguas, first recorded in the 1950s by the duo Garzon y Collazos (Wikipedia). The traditional choreography, created by folklorist Ines Garcia de Duran in 1960, has three basic steps (caminado, bambuqueado, contradanza) and eight figures depicting courtship. Anthem of the Festival Folclorico y Reinado Nacional del Bambuco in Neiva.
sanjuanero.insight: Though derived from bambuco with joropo influence, the Sanjuanero Huilense is widely considered Colombia's most representative folkloric dance and is the obligatory piece performed by contestants of the Reinado Nacional del Bambuco (Wikipedia; Gobernacion del Huila).
sanjuanero.image_significance: The festive bambuco of Neiva. A representative image shows colorful regional costume and lively partner or troupe footwork — Huila/Tolima, Colombia.

yumbada.name: Yumbada
yumbada.era: Pre-Hispanic origins; present Cotocollao ritual revived ~20 years ago
yumbada.tagline: Indigenous ritual dance-drama of forest 'yumbos' near Quito.
yumbada.profile: The Yumbada is an Indigenous (Kichwa) and mestizo ritual dance-drama performed in neighborhoods of Quito, most prominently Cotocollao and La Magdalena, each June around Corpus Christi and the solstice (Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana). Dancers personify 'yumbos,' shaman figures associated with the Amazonian/montane forest, led by a 'mamaco' or pingullero who plays a small drum and a three-note pingullo flute. The ritual climax is the 'Yumbo Huanuchiy' (Killing of the Yumbo), a dramatized murder and resurrection linked to healing, fertility and the mythic alliance of the Quitu and Cara peoples (Frank Salomon, IFEA; El Telegrafo). Dancers carry black chonta-palm lances and wear long wigs, ribbons, plumes and masks; it is treated as a sacred rite rather than folkloric spectacle.
yumbada.insight: Anthropologist Frank Salomon documented the Yumbada as a ritual drama; four yumbadas coexist today in Quito's Zona La Delicia (Rumicucho, Pomasqui, Tanlahua, Cotocollao), and the Cotocollao community pursued, then withdrew from, formal national heritage declaration, fearing folklorization (Salomon, IFEA; Quito Informa).
yumbada.image_significance: Ceremonial yumbo dance-drama. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Quito area, Ecuador.

bomba-del-chota.name: Bomba del Chota
bomba-del-chota.era: Colonial origins (late 16th-c. African slave labor); consolidated 19th-20th c.
bomba-del-chota.tagline: Afro-Ecuadorian drum, song and dance of the Chota Valley.
bomba-del-chota.profile: Bomba del Chota is the Afro-Ecuadorian music-and-dance tradition of the Chota-Mira valley on the Imbabura/Carchi border, in communities such as Carpuela, El Juncal, Chalguayacu and La Concepcion (English Wikipedia). The word 'bomba' names the goatskin drum, the genre, and the dance. Couples dance with marked hip movement; women are known for dancing while balancing a bottle on the head (the 'baile de la botella'). Music is built on quatrain coplas with guitar, guiro, requinto and the bomba drum, and a related ensemble, the banda mocha, uses improvised instruments such as dried gourd horns and leaves (Spanish Wikipedia; All Around This World).
bomba-del-chota.insight: Distinct from Puerto Rican bomba, the Ecuadorian bomba was certified part of Ecuador's Intangible Cultural Heritage by the INPC and Ministry of Culture on 20 October 2020 as 'La Bomba, musica, danza y saberes ancestrales' - the 18th manifestation certified within a national inventory of 8,327 (INPC).
bomba-del-chota.image_significance: Afro-Ecuadorian bottle-balancing dance. A representative image shows colorful regional costume and lively partner or troupe footwork — Chota Valley, Ecuador.

gato.name: Gato
gato.era: Emerged c. 1820s-1830s; peak gaucho popularity mid-19th century
gato.tagline: Playful, picaresque gaucho couple dance with humorous verses.
gato.profile: The gato ('cat') is a lively, picaresque couples folk dance and music style, hugely popular across rural Argentina and a favorite of gaucho culture. Its rhythm resembles the chacarera but its structure differs; couples perform stomping, spinning, finger-snapping and 'relaciones' (humorous recited couplets when the music stops). It is played on guitar with sung verses; variants include the gato cuyano, patriótico, valseado, and polqueado (English Wikipedia).
gato.insight: The gato was among the most popular dances of independence-era Argentina and strongly influenced the chacarera; Britannica lists it among the core gaucho couple dances based on the fandango (Encyclopædia Britannica).
gato.image_significance: The gauchos' picaresque couple dance. A representative image shows colorful regional costume and lively partner or troupe footwork — pampas, Argentina.

pericon.name: Pericon
pericon.era: Evolved late 18th-early 19th c. from cielito/contradanza; Pericón Nacional registered 1880s
pericon.tagline: Stately group square-dance of eight couples waving handkerchiefs.
pericon.profile: The pericón is a group folk dance of Argentina and Uruguay performed by a set of independent couples, generally eight, who execute coordinated contradance/quadrille figures at the shout of '¡Aura!' - including the famous 'pabellón,' where couples raise handkerchiefs to form a flag. Dancers wear colonial-era dress and carry pañuelos (Spanish Wikipedia; Plan Ceibal). It evolved from the cielito (a descendant of the British country dance) alongside the media caña.
pericon.insight: The pericón was declared the 'Danza Nacional Argentina' by Ley 26.297 (2007); the popular 'Pericón Nacional' score was registered by Gerardo Grasso in the late 1880s (Argentina InfoLeg; Spanish Wikipedia).
pericon.image_significance: The group star dance with a caller. A representative image shows colorful regional costume and lively partner or troupe footwork — Rio de la Plata, Argentina.

mwomboko.name: Mwomboko
mwomboko.profile: Mwomboko is a Kikuyu social partner dance of central Kenya that emerged in the colonial era, traced to roughly the late 1930s and 1940s (The Standard). It is danced in pairs with methodical, counted steps resembling a waltz or slow foxtrot, prominently featuring the accordion (kinanda kia mugeto) and the karing'aring'a (a metal ring idiophone). The style developed after veterans returning from the World Wars brought back accordions and guitars, and after the colonial ban on the protest dance Muthirigu pushed the community toward a tolerated substitute.
mwomboko.insight: Originally a dance for unmarried young men, mwomboko was later adopted by elders and is now showcased at Kenyan national celebrations such as Madaraka and Mashujaa Day; veterans like Wachira Waweru have warned the accordion-driven genre risks dying out (The Standard).
mwomboko.image_significance: Kikuyu foxtrot of the accordion. A representative image shows drum-driven communal movement, often in a circle with vivid textiles — Kikuyu, Kenya.

setapa.name: Setapa
setapa.tagline: Bangwaketse harvest dance of stamping, tapping feet
setapa.profile: Setapa is a traditional dance of the Bangwaketse tribe of Kanye and surrounding villages in southern Botswana, its name derived from the Setswana "go tapa-tapa," to step into the ground continuously (Wikipedia; Taste of Southern Africa). Performed by mixed groups in animal-skin costume (men in motseto briefs, women in diphaeyana skirts) with ankle rattles and oxhide sandals, it features intricate tapping footwork; variants include setapa sa dipitse (galloping-horse sound) and setapa sa go goga maoto (dragging feet). It celebrates the harvest season, letlhafula.
setapa.insight: Setapa is a celebratory harvest dance historically performed in all-night sessions in the fields and at the village kgotla; once a gendered form where girls sang and boys danced, today both men and women take part, and it has become widely performed across Tswana-speaking communities of southern Africa (Taste of Southern Africa).
setapa.image_significance: Tswana continuous-footwork dance. A representative image shows drum-driven communal movement, often in a circle with vivid textiles — Tswana (Bangwaketse), Botswana.

mokhibo.name: Mokhibo
mokhibo.profile: Mokhibo is the Basotho women's dance of Lesotho, performed from a kneeling position: dancers ripple and shake their shoulders, the body gently rising and falling as the hands sweep upward, while an informal choir behind them sings and claps (South Africa Online). Sometimes called the 'knee dance', its movements are said to echo women's kneeling work activities (Universal Tongue). It is performed at weddings, Christmas and cultural festivals, often to a male chorus's rhythmic chanting (South Africa Online).
mokhibo.insight: Mokhibo and the men's mohobelo are the two everyday Basotho social dances, distinct from the mokorotlo war/praise anthem performed for chiefs (South Africa Online).
mokhibo.image_significance: Women's kneeling shoulder dance. A representative image shows drum-driven communal movement, often in a circle with vivid textiles — Basotho, Lesotho.

verbunk.name: Verbunk
verbunk.profile: The hussar recruiting dance — Verbunk (Hungary). Full sourced 9-field A+ profile in research artifact W9; concise schema stub pending text expansion.
verbunk.image_significance: The hussar recruiting dance. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — Hungary.
verbunk.profile_long:
The Verbunk represents a pivotal shift in Hungarian dance history, marking the transition from medieval 'old stratum' dances to the 'new stratum' that defines the modern national image. Its name is a corruption of the German word 'Werbung,' meaning recruitment. During the mid-18th to early 19th centuries, the Habsburg military employed professional recruiters who traveled through villages with musicians. These recruiters performed the Verbunk to entice young peasants, offering a vision of the soldier's life as one of prestige, wealth, and physical mastery. The dance was so effective that it quickly moved beyond the barracks, becoming a favorite of both the noble elite and the peasantry during the Romantic era.

Structurally, the Verbunk is defined by its freedom. Unlike the rigid formations of Western European court dances, the Verbunk is largely improvisational, allowing a dancer to construct steps according to his 'mood and ingenuity,' as noted by ethnographers. While most variants are solo and irregular, some rare forms are performed in circles or semicircles, showing a distant relationship to the Alpine Schuhplattler. In a traditional village setting, the Verbunk serves as the ceremonial opening of a dance event, or 'táncciklus.' It establishes the rhythmic environment before the couple dances, such as the Csárdás, begin.

Technically, the dance is a display of rhythmic precision. In the mid-19th century, musicologist Theodor Billroth observed that Hungarian troops stationed in Vienna outperformed all other nationalities in their ability to keep time, a trait central to the Verbunk's execution. The movement vocabulary includes sharp leg-slapping, clicking of the heels, and intricate stamps that must align perfectly with the phrasing of the music. Though primarily a male tradition, some regions developed simplified versions for women, though the core of the tradition remains a display of male athletic prowess. Today, the dance is preserved through the global Táncház movement, ensuring that the 'itching soles' of the Hungarian tradition continue to perform these historical recruitment steps in a modern, celebratory context.

kaerajaan.name: Kaerajaan
kaerajaan.era: Origin tied to an 1889 mocking song from Laaniste/Ahja; documented as a dance by Anna Raudkats in the 1910s-1920s
kaerajaan.tagline: Estonia's best-known folk dance, born from a teasing song.
kaerajaan.profile: Kaerajaan (Kaera-Jaan, 'Oats-Jaan / John of Oats') is a lively couple/mixer folk dance from southeastern Estonia, linked musically and structurally to the European quadrille (Univ. of Tartu; Kapper). Its name comes from a teasing song about Jaan Matson, a blacksmith's apprentice at Ahja manor known as a ladies' man; the lyric begins 'Kaera-Jaan, Kaera-Jaan...' (Tartu 2024; Tallinn University). Typically accompanied by accordion and sung melody, it features prancing steps and partner figures and is among the most widely performed dances at Estonian celebrations and abroad; a popular stage arrangement was choreographed by Mait Agu.
kaerajaan.insight: Per Tartu 2024 (European Capital of Culture), the Laaniste blacksmith Jaan had no idea he inspired Estonia's best-known folk dance, still popular 135 years later; once thought purely original, kaerajaan was later recognized as linked to the international quadrille tradition (Tartu 2024; Kapper, Folklore 54).
kaerajaan.image_significance: The blacksmith's teasing couple dance. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — Estonia.

tuljak.name: Tuljak
tuljak.era: Music by Miina Harma 1897; dance by Anna Raudkats; at song celebrations from 1928, every Dance Celebration since 1934
tuljak.tagline: Estonia's celebratory wedding dance and Dance Celebration finale.
tuljak.profile: Tuljak is a popular Estonian couple dance of wedding-celebration character, telling the courting and wedding story of Tonn and Manni (All Around This World; Estonian Wikipedia). The choral song 'Tuljak' was composed by Miina Harma in 1897 as an arrangement of several folk melodies, with lyrics by Karl Ferdinand Karlson; Anna Raudkats created the accompanying dance, which draws on the Viru waltz and older dances (Estonian Music Information Centre; Miina Harma Gumnaasium). The traditional dance-tale of courtship was traced to Slavonic dances; the choreographed Tuljak has been the grand finale of every Estonian Dance Celebration, accompanied by choir and orchestra.
tuljak.insight: 'Tuljak' has been played at every dance and song celebration since 1934 and is so emblematic that Estonians compare it to the anthem-like 'Mu isamaa on minu arm' (ERR).
tuljak.image_significance: The Dance Festival's wedding anthem. A representative image shows folk dress and patterned partner or group figures — Estonia.

katrilli.name: Katrilli
katrilli.era: Quadrille forms reached Finland late 18th c.; widespread early/mid-19th c.; Karelian/Skolt forms from Russia late 19th c.
katrilli.tagline: Finland's quadrille - a square or two-line figure set-dance.
katrilli.profile: Katrilli is the Finnish quadrille, a contra/set dance performed in a square (four couples) or two opposing lines, derived from the French cotillion/contredanse and the broader quadrille family (Finnish Wikipedia; Kansantanssin Ystavat). Its turns (vuorot) combine standard figures - circles, vis-a-vis (vastuu), place-changes, pass-throughs (lapikaynti) and karkelo. Two waves reached Finland: a Swedish-derived 'ruotsinkatrilli' across most of the country and a Russian-derived form in Finnish/Russian Karelia and among the Skolt Sami. Steps range from walking and half-run to polka and waltz; Karelian katrillis often feature a male improvisation section (ripaska). Music is led by fiddle, accordion and harmonium.
katrilli.insight: Among Finnish dances recorded by collectors, katrillis are one of the most common types; since the 1980s the improvised 'huutokatrilli' (called/shouted quadrille) has become a late-night highlight at the Kaustinen Folk Music Festival (Finnish Wikipedia; kaustinen.net).

purpuri.name: Purpuri
purpuri.era: Arrived from the east early 19th c. (Oulu 1809, Helsinki 1820s); wedding centerpiece into the 1950s-60s; revived from early 1980s
purpuri.tagline: Finland's potpourri wedding suite of sequential figure dances.
purpuri.profile: Purpuri ('potpourri') is a suite of figure dances performed one after another, historically the principal ceremonial and social wedding dance - especially in Swedish-speaking Ostrobothnia (Kokkola, Kronoby, Nedervetil, Terjarv), western Uusimaa, Aboland and around Kaustinen (Wiki for Living Heritage; Finnish Music Quarterly). At three-day weddings, the 'rospurpuri' opened with a long polonaise ('rosa') danced by bridesmaids and groomsmen, paired by the bridal couple; later purpuris were public. It is accompanied by fiddle and by horn ensembles (e.g. Kronoby Hornkapell) when danced outdoors; the constituent dances draw on the quadrille, minuet, polska, polka and waltz.
purpuri.insight: The purpuri was so central that the seminal Kaustinen ensemble formed in 1946 and later led by Konsta Jylha (1910-1984) was named 'Purppuripelimannit'; tradition-bearers' later adoption of national costume for staged purpuri performances entwined the dance with folk-costume display (Wiki for Living Heritage; FMQ).

khanjluri.name: Khanjluri
khanjluri.profile: Khanjluri is a competitive war-themed dance in which shepherds dressed in red chokhas compete in dagger skills and complex movements, one performer replacing another to showcase courage and skill (Wikipedia; Sukhishvili). The Sukhishvili repertoire describes it as a dance depicting warriors' descent from the mountains with swords and knives, where dancers compete in rapidly performing the most complex feats. Because it involves daggers and knives thrown into the air, spun and used in combat-simulating maneuvers, it demands exceptional practice and precision (iberogeorgia).
khanjluri.insight: Khanjluri turns the Georgian warrior ethos into a wordless dialogue of dexterity and bravado, symbolizing the passing of martial tradition between generations; the name derives from 'khanjali' (dagger).
khanjluri.image_significance: Shepherds duel with daggers. A representative image shows upright carriage, sweeping arm lines and embroidered dress — Georgia.

tahtib.name: Tahtib (Tahteeb)
tahtib.era: ancient (Old Kingdom roots); festive form from the New Kingdom
tahtib.tagline: Ancient Egyptian stick art that became a festive dance
tahtib.profile: Tahtib (tahteeb) is an Egyptian stick art from Upper Egypt that blends martial art, fencing and dance. Per UNESCO, which inscribed it in 2016, it involves a brief, non-violent interchange between two men each wielding a long stick (asa) while folk music plays; no striking is allowed and complete control must be shown. Rooted in ancient Egypt - depicted on New Kingdom temple walls at Luxor and Saqqara - it survives as a festive game among Sa'idi communities, embodying values of respect, courage, chivalry and pride.
tahtib.insight: Tahtib is one of the oldest documented Egyptian performance traditions and the source of the women's Saidi cane dance; it is Egypt's UNESCO-listed intangible heritage, inscribed in 2016 (UNESCO; Egypt Museum).
tahtib.image_significance: The 4,000-year-old stick dance. A representative image shows a line or row formation, often with canes, swords or flowing veils — Upper Egypt, Egypt.

khaleegy.name: Khaleegy (Khaliji)
khaleegy.era: Traditional; music traced to Umayyad/Islamic period
khaleegy.tagline: Gulf women's hair-and-thobe dance swaying to khaleeji rhythms
khaleegy.profile: Khaleegy is a women's social folk dance of the Arabian Gulf - Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE, Qatar and Oman - performed in groups at weddings, engagements and holidays (Wikipedia). It is danced in a loose, richly embroidered overdress called the thobe al-nashal worn without a hip belt, emphasizing gliding footwork, shoulder shimmies, hand gestures and the rhythmic side-to-side tossing of long, unbound hair to khaleeji rhythms (Belly Dance Geek). The floating dress and hair are often linked to the region's maritime, pearl-diving and Bedouin heritage.
khaleegy.insight: Known in the UAE as raks al-nashal and in Kuwait as samri, it was traditionally danced privately in women-only gatherings; by the early 1980s famous Egyptian belly dancers including Sohair Zaki and Nagwa Fouad began incorporating stylized Khaleeji phrases into their stage shows (Suhaila International).
khaleegy.image_significance: The Gulf hair-toss dance. A representative image shows a line or row formation, often with canes, swords or flowing veils — Arabian Gulf, Gulf states.

moribayasa.name: Moribayasa
moribayasa.era: Very old traditional rhythm and dance
moribayasa.tagline: Malinke solo women's liberation and thanksgiving dance
moribayasa.profile: Moribayasa is a very old rhythm and dance of the Malinke (Mandinka) of northeastern Guinea, performed by a woman who has overcome a major hardship such as infertility or serious illness, fulfilling a vow (Tontinkan; Wikipedia). Such a vow can be taken only once in a lifetime. For the dance the woman wears old, torn clothes and is allowed to break taboos; accompanied by djembe and dunun, she dances around the village from one tree (often a mango or the 'Moribayasa' tree) to another, then buries or leaves the rags behind the tree (Mama Lisa; Mamady Keita, A Life for the Djembe).
moribayasa.insight: Master drummer Famoudou Konate and others spread Moribayasa internationally through workshops and tours; Mamady Keita's book documents that the vow is so significant a woman may take it only once (Grokipedia; thesmith.org.uk).

royal-ballet-of-cambodia.name: Royal Ballet of Cambodia (Apsara)
royal-ballet-of-cambodia.era: Linked to the Khmer court for over 1,000 years
royal-ballet-of-cambodia.tagline: Cambodia's sacred classical court dance of royal wealth
royal-ballet-of-cambodia.profile: The Royal Ballet of Cambodia (Robam Preah Reach Trop, "dance of royal wealth"), also called Khmer classical dance, is renowned for graceful hand gestures and elaborate costumes and has been associated with the Khmer court for over a thousand years (Wikipedia; UNESCO). Performed at coronations, weddings, funerals and Khmer holidays to a pinpeat ensemble with a sung narration, its repertory perpetuates legends of the Reamker; four character types exist — neang (woman), neayrong (man), yeak (giant) and sva (monkey).
royal-ballet-of-cambodia.insight: Infused with a sacred, symbolic role embodying refinement, respect and spirituality, the Royal Ballet practically ceased to exist under the Khmer Rouge, who killed almost all master dancers; it was proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO on November 7, 2003 (inscribed on the Representative List in 2008) and is cherished as the emblem of Khmer culture.
royal-ballet-of-cambodia.image_significance: Dance of the gods. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Khmer court, Cambodia.

reog-ponorogo.name: Reog Ponorogo
reog-ponorogo.tagline: East Javanese masked dance with the giant peacock-tiger mask
reog-ponorogo.profile: Reog Ponorogo is a centuries-old theatrical dance from the Ponorogo District of East Java that blends dance, music and mythology (UNESCO; ANTARA). Performers dress as kings, war commanders, knights and horse-mounted warriors to narrate the story of the Bantarangin Kingdom and its king. Its iconic centerpiece is the Dadak Merak (Singo Barong), a huge mask resembling a tiger's head topped with peacock feathers. Traditionally performed at disaster-aversion ceremonies, village cleansings, weddings, circumcisions, thanksgivings, Islamic and national holidays and to welcome guests, it is a source of community pride embodying courage and solidarity.
reog-ponorogo.insight: Reog Ponorogo was inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding on 3 December 2024 at the 19th Committee session in Asuncion, Paraguay - Indonesia's 14th element on UNESCO's lists - amid concern that Reog masters are increasingly hard to find (Tempo; UNESCO).
reog-ponorogo.image_significance: The peacock-tiger mask of Java. A representative image shows gilded costume, angular hand poses and a temple or court setting — East Java, Indonesia.

ori-tahiti.name: Ori Tahiti
ori-tahiti.tagline: The umbrella of all traditional Tahitian dance.
ori-tahiti.profile: Ori Tahiti ('Tahitian dance') is the umbrella term for the dance traditions of Tahiti and the Society Islands (Bora Bora, Moorea, Raiatea, Tahaa, Huahine). It unites five forms - oteea, aparima, hivinau, paoa and the recitative pataautau - characterized by a divided body (legs mark the percussion rhythm; arms/torso narrate a cultural theme), Tahitian-language song, percussion (toere, pahu) and plant-fiber costumes. Troupes (pupu ori) perform at the Heiva i Tahiti festival - founded in 1881 as 'Tiurai' and renamed Heiva in 1985 - functioning as social cohesion and identity transmission (culture.gouv.fr; Tahiti Tourisme).
ori-tahiti.insight: Banned under the 1819 Pomare Code, the dance was fully revived in 1956 when Madeleine Moua, a Papeete school principal, founded the troupe 'Heiva Tahiti'; the practice was added to France's national intangible-heritage inventory in 2017 (culture.gouv.fr).
ori-tahiti.image_significance: Tahiti's hip-shaking drum dance. A representative image shows grass or tapa attire and synchronized group motion in an open-air island setting — Society Islands, French Polynesia.
